documents.abstract: Commercial banks in Kenya have invested heavily in artificial intelligence (AI), yet sector profitability has weakened, with average return on assets (ROA) falling from 3.3 percent in 2021 to 2.6 percent in 2024. This research investigated the effect of AI adoption on the financial performance of commercial banks in Kenya. Specifically, it examined the effects of AI-enabled customer service, machine learning credit scoring, robotic process automation and AI-driven fraud detection on financial performance, measured by ROA, as well as the mediating effect of operational efficiency and the moderating effect of bank size. A census of all 38 commercial banks licensed by the Central Bank of Kenya was undertaken, using data from audited annual reports and Central Bank of Kenya supervisory returns. Data were analysed using random effects panel regression with cluster-robust standard errors, the causal steps approach supplemented by the Sobel test, and moderated regression. AI-enabled customer service had a positive and significant effect on ROA (β = 0.927, p = 0.003). Machine learning credit scoring (β = −0.046, p = 0.841), robotic process automation (β = −0.450, p = 0.098) and AI-driven fraud detection (β = 0.137, p = 0.459) had no significant effects. AI-enabled customer service lowered the cost-to-income ratio (β = −0.194, p < 0.001), but operational efficiency did not significantly mediate its relationship with ROA (Sobel z = 1.287, p = 0.198). The interaction between AI adoption and bank size was not significant (β = 0.154, p = 0.589). The study concluded that the effect of AI adoption on bank performance is application-specific. Only customer-facing AI translated into higher profitability, while the credit scoring, process automation and fraud detection applications did not. Operational efficiency did not mediate, and bank size did not moderate, the connection between AI adoption and performance.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming tourism destinations through personalized services, conversational and generative interfaces, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making. Yet technology adoption alone does not explain how destinations convert AI-generated information into coordinated managerial action. Objective: This study addresses that organizational problem through a conceptual integrative review of research on AI-enabled tourism services, smart destination management, destination governance, visitor experience, organizational capabilities, workforce readiness, and responsible data practices. Methods: The synthesis identifies four interconnected application domains: AI-driven personalization, conversational and generative visitor interaction, predictive visitor-flow analytics, and data-driven destination governance. These domains are abstracted into the AI-Enabled Smart Destination Management (AI-SDM) framework, which connects AI-Enabled Service Capability, Smart Destination Governance Capability, and Visitor Experience Outcomes. Results: Visitor and operational intelligence functions as the principal conversion input, while visitor-generated behavioral and experiential feedback supports subsequent organizational learning and AI adaptation. Workforce AI Readiness and Responsible Data Governance are positioned as enabling conditions. The framework contributes to destination-management theory by shifting attention from AI adoption toward the organizational capability required to sense relevant visitor information, interpret and coordinate responses, and responsibly convert intelligence into destination action and visitor value. It complements broad smart-tourism and emerging cognitive-destination architectures by specifying the organizational intelligence-to-action mechanism that links AI-enabled interactions with destination governance and learning. Conclusion: The paper concludes with propositions and an empirical research agenda for measurement development and validation.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies are transforming advanced manufacturing by enabling intelligent, data-driven, and sustainable production systems. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the synergistic integration of AI algorithms with cyber-physical Digital Twin frameworks across key manufacturing domains, including additive manufacturing, microwave hybrid heating, robotic machining, and metal cladding. AI-driven models facilitate real-time defect detection, predictive maintenance, adaptive process control, and parameter optimization, while Digital Twins provide high-fidelity virtual replicas for simulation, synchronization, and closed-loop decision-making. The convergence of these technologies enables predictive and prescriptive manufacturing strategies, reducing waste, improving energy efficiency, and enhancing product quality. Furthermore, the study examines system-level integration architectures, cloud–edge computing infrastructure, and emerging approaches such as physics-informed neural networks and federated learning. The transition toward Industry 5.0 is discussed, emphasizing human-centricity, sustainability, and ethical AI deployment. The findings highlight AI–DT integration as a foundational pillar for intelligent, resilient, and environmentally responsible manufacturing ecosystems.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Whether artificial intelligence (AI) alleviates or aggravates resource constraints is an open and increasingly consequential question: AI carries a substantial energy and water footprint, yet it may also raise resource-use efficiency through prediction, intelligent optimization, and better allocation. Using a balanced panel of 30 Chinese provinces over 2011–2024, this study measures green water-use efficiency (GWUE) with a Super-SBM model and estimates the association between AI development and GWUE using two-way fixed effects, complemented by an instrumental-variable strategy and interpretable machine learning. We find that AI development is associated with a significant improvement in GWUE: a one-standard-deviation increase in the AI index corresponds to a 3.8% rise in GWUE. The relationship is consistent with two channels—green technological innovation and environmental-governance capacity. The association is stronger where per-capita water use is higher, and differs across regions of differing industrial water dependence and computing infrastructure. XGBoost–SHAP analysis further suggests a nonlinear transition around an AI development level of approximately 0.12, beyond which AI’s marginal contribution to predicted GWUE becomes increasingly positive. These findings indicate that AI does not automatically become a green technology; its resource-efficiency dividend depends on the resource and technological environment in which it is deployed.

Rational nanoparticle design, stimuli-responsive release control, and release kinetics matching with changing tissue microenvironment are improving preclinical and clinical regenerative therapy results and clinical translation utilizing artificial intelligence and machine learning. This review is intended to explore the use of interdisciplinary strategies that integrate computational design and experimental validation to advance tissue-focused drug delivery systems. Using AI-enabled procedures to increase encapsulation efficiencies and tunability of release and target engagement has led to the acceleration of the inverse design and closed-loop optimization processes in numerous preclinical models. Unfortunately, sparse metadata and tiny heterogeneous datasets restrained repeatability. Incompetent benchmark repositories, inconsistent reporting, and data sharing pipelines. The regulatory paths for algorithm-informed device-drug products are new and require models, quantification of uncertainty, sterilization validation, and clinical-grade stability data. The pragmatic roadmap emphasizes short-term metadata standards, intermediate community-based benchmarks, and long-term adaptive clinical trials linking computational outcomes with biomarker-driven goals. A consolidated series of technical, translational, and governance recommendations is presented with an actionable checklist made for bridging computational design with clinical translation, such as a synthesis of governance and experiments checklist, which has never been seen before, for faster real-world implementation.

Background and Aims: Mental health disorders constitute a major global health burden, while mental health services remain inadequately resourced, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, have opened new possibilities for the early detection, diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of mental health conditions. Despite rapid growth, research in this field is highly interdisciplinary and fragmented, limiting understanding of its overall development. Methods: A retrospective cross-sectional bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Scopus database. Peer-reviewed journal articles published between January 1, 2004, and December 31, 2024, were retrieved through title-based searches combining AI- and mental health-related terms. Bibliometric indicators, including publication output, authors, institutions, countries, journals, funding agencies, and highly cited articles, were analyzed. Science-mapping techniques and network visualization using VOS viewer were employed to explore intellectual, social, and conceptual research structures. Results: A total of 14,904 publications were included. Research growth was modest until 2015 but accelerated markedly after 2019 (R² = 0.9685). The field was dominated by medicine, neuroscience, and computer science. The United States, China, and the United Kingdom emerged as the leading contributors in both productivity and international collaboration. Key research hotspots included AI-driven neuroimaging, natural language processing for mental health assessment, social media–based surveillance, and digital mental health interventions. Conclusion: AI research in mental health has expanded rapidly, progressing from neurobiological modeling to scalable digital applications. Future advancement will require ethical governance, representative datasets, interdisciplinary collaboration, and robust clinical validation to ensure safe, effective, and equitable implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Conventional crop breeding has delivered substantial yield and quality gains but faces persistent constraints from long breeding cycles, limited genetic diversity, and increasing climate volatility. Artificial intelligence (AI) and synthetic biology (SynBio) are emerging as complementary technologies that can accelerate allele discovery, trait design, and deployment across major staples and under-researched crops. Machine learning, computer vision, and robotics support high-throughput phenotyping from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery and mobile devices, while genomic prediction models that integrate multi-omics and climate data can improve selection accuracy for traits such as yield stability and stress tolerance. SynBio platforms enable precise genome editing, synthetic circuits, and metabolic pathway engineering, with applications ranging from biofortified rice to multiplex editing in maize and pangenome-informed breeding in orphan crops such as chickpea and pearl millet. Their convergence, often described as “Breeding 5.0,” supports AI-guided design–build–test–learn (DBTL) cycles that optimize ideotypes for resource efficiency, resilience, and nutrition while reducing reliance on agrochemical inputs. This narrative review outlines the evolution from classical to molecular breeding, synthesizes current AI–SynBio pipelines with illustrative case studies, and highlights persistent challenges in data quality, transformation efficiency, biosafety, regulatory harmonization, and equitable access. We conclude with priorities for inclusive innovation to ensure that climate-smart, nutritious crops benefit diverse agroecosystems responsibly.

Professional autonomy is a foundational ethical principle in healthcare, underpinning healthcare professionals’ capacity to exercise independent clinical judgement in light of a patient's particular circumstances, preferences and needs. While ethical debate surrounding medical AI has focused extensively on safety, accuracy and bias, its implications for professional autonomy have received comparatively less attention, a notable omission given AI's growing role in shaping clinical decision-making. This article identifies three salient mechanisms through which AI integration may constrain professional autonomy: (1) algorithmic opacity and explainability, (2) automation bias and de-skilling and (3) institutional pressures. Whilst proposed safeguards such as explainable AI, professional training, system design and institutional governance represent important directions, they do not yet adequately protect professional autonomy. This article therefore calls for closer scrutiny of current approaches to AI integration and for governance frameworks that attend not only to the technical properties of AI systems, but to the organisational and institutional conditions in which they are deployed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This research evaluates the negative impacts of Artificial Intelligence dependency on the cognitive and academic development of students within the Cameroonian higher education landscape. Utilizing a multiple case study design to facilitate literal replication across diverse settings, this study analyzed data collected from students at the University of Yaoundé, the University of Bamenda, and Yaoundé International Business School. A total of 525 students were surveyed using a purposive sampling strategy to account for the unique dynamics of public university massification and private sector specialization in Cameroon. The findings indicate a high prevalence of AI utilization, with 85.3% of respondents reporting daily or weekly usage for academic tasks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Diabetes mellitus can lead to long-term disability through complications affecting vision, mobility, kidney function, neurologic recovery, physical capacity, and cognition.This review examined how artificial intelligence (AI) supports early detection, risk prediction, and prevention-oriented decision support across diabetesrelated disability pathways.PubMed and Google Scholar were searched through 14 February 2026 using a two-stage strategy combining contextual disability evidence with AI-focused searches.Eligible studies were English-language human studies with accessible full text and relevance to predefined disability pathways; AI-focused studies additionally required explicit use of AI, machine learning, deep learning, or computational decision support.The merged corpus included 101 studies: 38 contextual non-AI studies and 63 AI-focused studies.Diagnostic and detection evidence was appraised using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2-informed criteria, prediction and prognostic evidence using the Prediction model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool-informed criteria, and heterogeneous findings were synthesized narratively.The strongest AI evidence concerned diabetic retinopathy, diabetic foot complications, and diabetic kidney disease, whereas neuropathy-related falls, frailty, sarcopenia, and cognitive decline were less mature and less frequently externally validated.Overall, evidence is stronger for detection and risk prediction than for demonstrated prevention of disability.Clinical translation therefore requires external validation, calibration, transportability, workflow integration, and prospective evaluation of patient-centered disability outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of online services, digital education and large-scale artificial intelligence has increased the electricity demand of cloud data centres, where servers, storage, networks and cooling equipment run around the clock. Rule-based management policies, which react to fixed thresholds, often leave servers underused and cooling plants over-provisioned. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a different approach: models learn from operational data, anticipate demand and choose actions that save energy while protecting service quality. This review examines how AI is applied to four tasks in a green data centre: forecasting workload, allocating and consolidating virtual machines, scheduling tasks with awareness of energy and carbon, and controlling cooling systems. Statistical forecasting, recurrent neural networks, reinforcement learning and data-driven cooling control are explained and compared through representative studies. An AI-based green-cloud framework is then described that combines a learning-based demand predictor, an energy- and carbon-aware scheduler, a cooling optimiser and a renewable-supply monitor in a closed control loop. A simulation-based evaluation plan using energy, response time, utilization and carbon emission as metrics is outlined. Challenges including data quality, model interpretability, safety of autonomous control and the energy cost of the AI models themselves are discussed.

In today’s rapidly evolving business environment, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a transformative technological capability with profound implications for strategic decision-making and modern business management. The growing ability of AI systems to analyse extensive volumes of structured and unstructured data, detect intricate patterns, produce predictive insights, and automate analytical activities is reshaping the processes through which organisations formulate and implement strategic decisions. Through the review of recent literature and real-world case studies, this paper critically argues that AI is fundamentally reshaping strategic decision-making and presents a reasoned perspective on how this shift is transforming business management practices and competitive strategies in contemporary organisations. This study also explores the challenges and risks of AI-driven strategic decision-making. The study concludes that the greatest value of AI lies in its capacity to augment rather than replace managerial intelligence. Hence, the study recommends that organisations should adopt hybrid decision-making by combining AI-generated insights with human expertise to enhance decision accuracy, critical thinking, and strategic judgement.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies, cloud computing, interconnected networks, and online services has significantly increased the complexity of modern cybersecurity challenges. Organizations increasingly face sophisticated cyber threats, including malware infections, ransomware, phishing campaigns, unauthorized network intrusions, insider threats, and advanced persistent threats (APTs). Traditional cybersecurity mechanisms, which primarily depend on predefined rules, signature-based detection, and manual security monitoring, often struggle to identify previously unknown attacks and respond effectively to rapidly evolving threats. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), natural language processing (NLP), and behavioral analytics, has emerged as a promising approach for strengthening cybersecurity capabilities.This review examines the application of AI-driven technologies in modern cybersecurity, emphasizing intelligent threat detection, cyberattack prevention, and information security. It explores the role of machine learning and deep learning in network intrusion detection, malware classification, phishing identification, anomaly detection, behavioral threat analysis, and automated incident response. Furthermore, the review investigates emerging developments in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), adversarial machine learning, federated learning, and generative AI, highlighting their implications for developing more adaptive and resilient security infrastructures. Recent academic research published in 2024 and 2025 is considered to evaluate technological developments, practical applications, and emerging limitations.The review identifies several important challenges affecting the practical adoption of AI-based cybersecurity systems, including data quality, model interpretability, false-positive detection, privacy concerns, adversarial manipulation, computational requirements, and the limited generalizability of models across different network environments. The analysis suggests that AI should complement, rather than completely replace, conventional security controls and human cybersecurity expertise. A layered cybersecurity architecture integrating AI-based detection, explainable decision support, continuous model monitoring, and human-supervised incident response may provide a more reliable approach to protecting modern digital environments. Finally, the paper identifies research opportunities related to adversarial robust AI, privacy-preserving collaborative learning, trustworthy generative AI, and autonomous cyber defense.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy by supporting lesion detection, characterization, and clinical decision-making.This narrative review summarizes current evidence on AI-assisted GI endoscopy, focusing on clinical applications, diagnostic performance, implementation challenges, and future directions.Machine learning and deep learning underpin computer-aided detection systems that identify suspicious lesions and computer-aided diagnosis systems that support their characterization.In colorectal cancer screening, the reviewed evidence highlights improvements in adenoma detection and the potential of AI to support optical diagnosis of colorectal polyps.In upper GI endoscopy, promising applications include the detection of Barrett's esophagus-associated neoplasia, early gastric cancer, and other premalignant lesions.Integration with image-enhanced endoscopy further supports real-time tissue characterization and risk stratification.Beyond lesion recognition, AI applications extend to procedural planning, quality assessment, and clinical decision support.Across these applications, data quality, external validation, and algorithm transparency remain central considerations when interpreting diagnostic performance and assessing clinical applicability.The review therefore emphasizes that successful implementation requires both technical development and careful evaluation within clinical workflows, alongside appropriate ethical and regulatory oversight.AI has substantial potential to advance precision endoscopy; however, its contribution to improved patient outcomes requires further clinical evaluation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly discussed through frameworks of adoption, automation, and organisational reinvention. Their application to higher education requires careful consideration of what education is intended to achieve. This reflective commentary examines McKinsey's three horizons of AI transformation through my experiences in ecological research, university teaching, postgraduate supervision, and academic writing. It develops ten connected arguments concerning scientific foundations, independent learning, field experience, curiosity, institutional resilience, academic conscience, respectful leadership, educational relationships, environmental responsibility, and selective adoption. Selected empirical studies and foundational ecological literature support the discussion, while personal judgments are distinguished from established findings. I argue that faster production of academic material alone cannot demonstrate deeper understanding or stronger research competence. AI can help when its use aligns with learning objectives and is supported by verification, fair assessment, and accountable human decisions. Risks include dependence on generated explanations, weakening of observational skills, restriction of exploratory inquiry, unfair judgments about authorship, increased workload, unequal access, and environmental costs. An ecological perspective also encourages attention to relationships, feedback, and institutions' ability to function when technological services fail. I propose that universities assess AI by what students can explain independently, how reliably they engage with evidence, and the quality of educational relationships. The central responsibility is to preserve the conditions that enable people to become capable researchers and conscientious members of society.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly transformed human resource management (HRM) from an administrative function into a strategic decision-making process, creating a critical need to balance algorithmic effectiveness with operational challenges. The purpose of this study is to explore the evolving integration of artificial intelligence within human resource management. This paper utilizes a bibliometric analysis using PRISMA reporting flow guidelines, analyzing data retrieved from the Scopus database for the period from 2015 to 2025. The results reveal an exponential expansion of scientific research over the decade. Out of an initial set of 2,949 publications, 622 relevant documents met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using VOSviewer. Annual publications grew from nine articles in 2015 to 218 articles in 2025. The geographical distribution shows that India leads the field with 116 publications, followed by China (114) and the United States (98). Furthermore, the thematic mapping identifies nine distinct clusters, with AI and human resource management standing out as the primary domains experiencing transformation. The findings confirm that the field has become a consolidated, dynamic discipline, with strategic implications for organizations seeking to align technological efficiency with organizational justice, ethical considerations, and employee well-being.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities to enhance medical imaging in pediatric oncology through quantitative image analysis and clinical decision support. This mini review examines the emerging role of AI in pediatric head and neck tumor imaging, including applications in lesion detection and characterization, tumor segmentation and volumetric analysis, treatment planning, longitudinal surveillance, prognostication, and precision medicine. Particular attention is given to the challenges of translating these approaches to pediatric populations, where rare and heterogeneous tumors, limited datasets, variable imaging protocols, and insufficient multicenter validation remain important barriers. We also discuss emerging strategies that may facilitate clinical translation, including federated learning, multimodal data integration, explainable AI, and integration with existing radiology workflows. Although pediatric-specific evidence remains limited, continued multicenter collaboration and prospective validation may enable AI-based tools to provide more reproducible quantitative imaging assessment and increasingly personalized clinical decision support. Ultimately, the clinical value of these technologies will depend on their ability to augment radiologist expertise and improve patient care through responsible integration into routine practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing diagnostic radiology, but education and training have not kept pace. This narrative review brings together current evidence on AI-supported learning in radiology education and how such learning can move into clinical innovation. Surveys from different countries point to the same gap: in a 25-country international survey of radiographers, radiologists, and students, only 10.3% had received formal AI training; in one national survey of Turkish residents, 84.5% had received none. The review maps competency frameworks and curriculum models that define AI literacy and support staged integration into residency. It also assesses AI as a teaching tool, including AI-assisted case-based learning, computer-aided diagnosis training, precision-education knowledge recommenders, and virtual, augmented, and extended reality. Controlled and randomized studies show measurable gains: computer-aided diagnosis training raised resident scores above self-study controls (mean score 52 vs. 38 on a 100-point scale), while an AI-based knowledge recommender shortened reporting time by 162 s per case and relative improvement in graded reporting accuracy scores of 14% (95% CI 8.1–19.8%). Large language models are promising but limited: GPT-4 approaches board-style examination performance (80.6%) yet remains poor at image-based reasoning (47.8%). The review closes by considering how education can feed clinical innovation, along with algorithmic and automation bias, ethical governance, and future research needs. AI education should therefore span the full continuum-from undergraduate training to continuing professional development-if radiology is to innovate safely, effectively, and equitably.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in spinal diagnostics, particularly through machine learning and deep learning applied to medical imaging and clinical data. These technologies may improve the detection and classification of spinal disorders, automate image interpretation and support clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current applications of AI in spinal diagnostics, focusing on methods for detecting spinal cord injuries, spinal tumors, degenerative spine diseases and vertebral fractures, as well as predicting treatment outcomes and postoperative complications. It also examines convolutional and recurrent neural networks, automated image segmentation and other machine learning approaches for analyzing spinal images and clinical information. Available evidence suggests that AI models can perform comparably to conventional methods and expert assessments and may exceed them in some settings. However, implementation remains limited by challenges related to dataset quality and diversity, model generalizability and interpretability, data privacy and regulatory and ethical considerations. This review highlights both the clinical potential of AI and the major barriers to its integration into routine spinal diagnostic practice. Further prospective validation, external testing across diverse patient populations and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to establish the clinical utility and ensure the safe implementation of AI-based spinal diagnostic tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly relevant to healthcare delivery, clinical training, and health professions education. Evidence from conflict-affected settings remains limited, despite workforce shortages, disrupted training pathways, and constrained digital infrastructure. This study assessed AI knowledge, trust, willingness, and digital capability among Syrian adults and healthcare respondents (students and qualified professionals), with emphasis on implications for AI literacy and professional education. We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of Syrian adults from March 4th to May 31st 2026, using a 35-item questionnaire distributed via social media through convenience sampling. The survey assessed AI awareness, trust, willingness, perceived risks and benefits, barriers to healthcare and digital health use, and Digital Literacy. Healthcare respondents (students and qualified professionals) completed additional items on clinical AI use and exposure to unsafe AI recommendations. Composite scores were calculated for AI Trust (3–15), AI Willingness (4–20), and Digital Literacy (2–10). Internal consistency was acceptable to excellent across scales (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.787–0.856). Among 829 participants, 353 (42.6%) were healthcare respondents (119 students and 234 qualified professionals). Mean AI Willingness, AI Trust, and Digital Literacy scores were 14.5 (SD 3.25), 11.0 (SD 2.34), and 6.67 (SD 1.80), respectively. In multivariable linear regression, AI Trust (β = 0.483) and Digital Literacy (β = 0.305) were the strongest predictors, followed by General AI Knowledge (β = 0.165). In sensitivity models excluding the Willingness item that loaded on Trust, Trust (β = 0.44 and 0.38) and Digital Literacy (β = 0.31 and 0.33) remained the strongest correlates. Educational use was the most accepted AI application (65.5%) and educational support was the leading perceived benefit (64.2%). Medical errors were the most frequently perceived risk (76.6%), while cost, unreliable internet access, and lack of Arabic-language content were major implementation barriers. In this online convenience sample, Trust and Digital Literacy were the strongest independent correlates of Willingness to use AI, followed by AI knowledge. The high acceptance of educational AI suggests a practical entry point for conflict-affected health systems. AI literacy should be integrated into undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing health professions education, with explicit training on critical appraisal, safe use, bias, privacy, local validation, and clinician oversight.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: High-temperature high-entropy alloys (HTHEAs) provide a large compositional space for tuning phase constitution, microstructure, elevated-temperature strength, creep resistance, and oxidation behavior. Their design is difficult for the same reason: performance depends on processing history, microstructure, temperature, loading mode, exposure time, and environment as well as nominal chemistry. Artificial-intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) methods are increasingly used to navigate this coupled space. This structured narrative review is organized around service-relevant high-temperature evidence rather than algorithm families, covering phase and microstructure stability, elevated-temperature strength, creep, oxidation, and the extent to which AI-selected alloys have been experimentally validated under the intended conditions. Evidence is assessed from internal statistical validation and physics-based filtering to alloy synthesis, direct high-temperature testing, extended service-relevant exposure, and iterative experiment–model feedback. Prospective studies now include tests of model-selected refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) at 800–1200 ∘C, a 149 h creep-rupture validation of an ML-designed high-entropy superalloy (HESA) at 1023 K and 480 MPa, and active-learning campaigns coupled directly to 1000 ∘C oxidation experiments. Across these examples, the limiting factors are concrete: many records lack exposure time, atmosphere, loading mode, measured composition, or post-test microstructure; compression data still outweigh tensile and creep evidence; and few AI-selected alloys have been followed through long-duration service-relevant tests.

Systematic literature review, conducted according to Kitchenham and Charters (2007) and reported following PRISMA 2020, that analyzes the artificial intelligence (AI) techniques used in assistive solutions to support the learning of students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and dyslexia, their purposes and the reported results. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and ERIC, complemented by backward reference searching. Undergraduate thesis (Computer Science, Universidade do Extremo Sul Catarinense – Unesc, Brazil). This registration is retrospective: the protocol was defined before the searches, but it is being registered after the searches (September 2, 2026), study selection and data extraction were completed.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid-β plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles, necessitating early and accurate diagnosis for effective intervention. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have significantly enhanced the discovery and interpretation of AD biomarkers by enabling the integration of complex, multimodal datasets, including neuroimaging, molecular, genetic, and digital biomarkers. AI-driven approaches, particularly machine learning and deep learning, have demonstrated high accuracy in identifying early pathological changes, predicting disease progression, and distinguishing AD from mild cognitive impairment. Emerging digital biomarkers derived from speech, motor activity, cognitive tests, and wearable sensors further expand non-invasive diagnostic capabilities. Despite promising results, challenges such as data heterogeneity, lack of external validation, limited interpretability ("black-box" models), and difficulties in clinical translation remain substantial barriers. Future research is expected to focus on multimodal data fusion, explainable AI, longitudinal modelling, and personalized prediction frameworks, along with improved standardization and regulatory validation. AI-based biomarker research holds potential to transform early diagnosis, prognosis, and precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.

Background Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is one of the most common chronic respiratory complications in preterm infants. Early identification of high-risk patients is essential for individualizing preventive strategies and optimizing therapeutic decisions. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models have emerged as promising tools to improve predictive performance in this population. Objective To evaluate and synthesize the predictive performance of AI-based models for BPD development in preterm infants and to assess their methodological quality. Methods A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA recommendations. We searched PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane Library up to February 2026. Studies developing or validating AI-based models for predicting BPD in preterm infants born at <32 weeks of gestation and/or with a birth weight < 1,500 g were included. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the PROBAST tool. Results Eighteen studies were included. Random Forest and XGBoost were the most frequently used algorithms. AUC values for the best-performing models ranged from 0.80 to 1.00, showing improved performance as postnatal variables were incorporated. However, the PROBAST assessment revealed a high overall risk of bias in 72.2% of the studies, primarily due to deficiencies in the analysis domain. Clinical applicability raised high concern in 38.9% of the studies due to a lack of external validation and heterogeneity in outcome definitions. Conclusions AI-based models show high discriminative capacity for BPD prediction; however, they have not yet demonstrated clear superiority over conventional statistical models in robust comparisons. Their routine clinical implementation is currently limited by poor methodological quality and scarce external validation. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261466494 , PROSPERO: CRD420261466494, registered retrospectively on August 4, 2026.

Cancer immunotherapy has transformed medical oncology, while individual’s therapeutic response to treatment is difficult because of the diverse nature and features of tumors and low precision and accuracy of markers, such as PD-L1, Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB), and Microsatellite Instability (MSI). Artificial intelligence integrates different types of data to cover the complexity of tumor-immune biological mechanisms. This review summarizes the recent studies in AI application in biomarker discovery and cancer immunotherapy prediction from a pan-cancer perspective, summarizing AI techniques, data types, clinical performance metrics, and implementation barriers. Selected AI-derived biomarkers have demonstrated promising performance compared with conventional biomarkers in specific studies. Indeed, selected AI-derived biomarkers demonstrated moderate-to-high discriminatory performance while reported estimates varied according to cancer type, prediction endpoint, and validation design. Deep Learning has shown promising results in Digital Pathology and Radiomics via providing tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes quantification and spatial immune phenotyping. Meanwhile, multi-omics integration frameworks, such as graph neural networks and transformer-based models can reveal complex associations among genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data. AI has indicated promising results in predicting both primary and acquired resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors, stratifying potential patients for immunotherapy, and predicting immune-related adverse events. Post-hoc explainability methods, including SHAP and LIME, can provide feature-attribution information, although their outputs should not be interpreted as causal or mechanistic explanations. The intersection of artificial intelligence and cancer immunotherapy is opening new roads for precision-oncology. However, the clinical translation of AI-driven biomarkers requires robust external validation, standardized methodologies, and evaluation across diverse patient populations.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven governance systems increasingly regulate seller decisions in cross-border e-commerce platforms. Mainstream research has treated AI-driven control intensity as a monotonically positive lever for platform coordination and seller outcomes. Aim: This study examines whether AI-driven governance intensity exhibits a non-linear performance boundary and identifies the mechanism under which governance expansion becomes counterproductive. Setting: The study was conducted among cross-border sellers on Amazon Global Selling, Alibaba International, and Shopee across China, Southeast Asia, and Eastern Europe. Method: Survey data from 207 cross-border sellers were analysed by using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5000-resample bootstrapping. Nonlinearity was confirmed by using a dual-condition criterion and a one-sided monotonicity test. Results: An inverted-U relationship emerged between AI governance intensity and seller performance (b_linear = 0.28, p = 0.021; b_quadratic = −0.19, p = 0.038), with a performance-reversing threshold at x* = 4.16 (bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] 95% confidence interval: [3.9, 4.5]). Excessive governance suppresses independent strategic learning (b = −0.34, p < 0.001), partially mediating the performance penalty (indirect = −0.16; direct = 0.14, p = 0.046). Market volatility amplifies the post-threshold effect (b = 0.19, p = 0.014), with 23% of sampled sellers in the substitution regime. Conclusion: Governance intensity must be calibrated relative to a structural threshold beyond which automation displaces the strategic-learning capability on which competitive performance depends. Contribution: This study contributes a regime-contingent threshold model showing that AI-driven governance intensity and seller performance follow an inverted-U relationship, with a performance-reversing threshold at x* = 4.16. Strategic-learning suppression is empirically confirmed as the erosion mechanism (partial mediation, indirect effect = −0.16), and market volatility amplifies the post-threshold penalty, grounded in dynamic capabilities theory and offering platform designers a calibration boundary rather than a general prescription.

The development of pharmaceutical formulations is changing. It is moving away from trial-anderror ways. Now modern approaches rely on science and data. Quality by Design or QbD offers a structured way to develop medicines. It starts with defining the Quality Target Product Profile or QTPP. Then it identifies Critical Quality Attributes or CQAs. It also looks at Critical Material Attributes or CMAs and Critical Process Parameters or CPPs. Design of Experiments or DoE helps in planning studies. This leads to the creation of a design space and a control strategy. Traditional QbD methods may not work well when variables are complex. They may not handle effects or strong interactions between factors. Artificial intelligence machine learning and predictive models can help. These tools can find patterns in data from experiments, formulations and manufacturing. This review looks at how AI fits into every stage of formulation development. It covers preformulation excipient selection, compatibility prediction, formulation optimization and predicting CQAs. It also includes identifying CMAs and CPPs. AI helps with process monitoring, Process Analytical Technology or PAT design space development and control strategy design. Applications are shown in solid dosage forms, modified-release systems, nanoparticulate and lipid-based formulations, continuous manufacturing, personalized medicines and 3D-printed medicines. Some challenges exist. These include data, overfitting models, models that are hard to understand lack of validation difficulties in scaling up regulatory issues and the need for diverse expertise. New ideas, like twins, continuous process verification, hybrid models that combine mechanics and AI generative AI and federated learning may push the field forward. In the end AI should support science not replace it. Experimental verification and mechanistic understanding are still essential.

Background Regulatory entry and public experience describe different aspects of artificial intelligence-enabled healthcare access. Methods This health policy study compares institutional arrangements in China, the United States, and the European Union, examines the coverage of equity-related evidence, and analyses an online Chinese survey. Of 480 submissions, 430 passed an attention check, including 32 respondents without reported functional contact and 398 entering the experience models. Results The institutional comparison identifies differences in regulatory objects, information recipients, and responsibility allocation. The coverage analysis distinguishes institutional information and hospital governance from measured portal use and service experience. In the survey, lower-capability respondents reported greater entry and operational barriers; 79 of 159 reported reducing or abandoning use because of barriers. Among contacted respondents, functional contact intensity was positively associated with perceived process ease (standardized β = 0.496), which was associated with perceived health-service responsiveness (standardized β = 0.381). The contact-by-capability interaction was negative (B = −0.254), contrary to the hypothesized direction. Conclusion The findings highlight entry and operational barriers alongside differences in experience among existing users, supporting evaluation of both access conditions and service encounters.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in shaping customer experiences and consumer consciousness. It explores how AI-generated interactions often transcend direct reflections of reality, creating immersive and dynamic experiential constructs that influence how consumers perceive, feel, and interpret value. The chapter highlights key areas including AI’s application in marketing, the importance of context and embodiment in AI interactions, and the evolving methodologies for consumer research enabled by AI. It also addresses critical ethical considerations such as privacy, transparency, and algorithmic bias. By analysing how AI modulates anticipatory structures, this work underscores AI’s role not merely as a tool for automation but as an active participant in the co-construction of subjective experience. Finally, the chapter outlines future research directions focused on consumer autonomy, cultural differences, emotional AI, and the societal impacts of AI integration. It concludes that responsible, context-aware deployment of AI is essential for businesses to foster trust and enrich customer experiences in an increasingly AI-mediated marketplace.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported nutrition guidance is increasingly becoming an accessible source of dietary information for university students; however, its relationship with healthy dietary habits and the potential mediating role of nutrition literacy require further investigation. This study examines the relationship between AI-supported nutrition guidance and healthy dietary habits among university students in Pakistan, with nutrition literacy as a potential mediator. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was proposed, involving 327 undergraduate and postgraduate students recruited through non-probability convenience sampling. Primary data were planned to be collected through a self-administered structured questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The questionnaire assessed AI-supported nutrition guidance, nutrition literacy, healthy dietary habits, and demographic characteristics. The proposed statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression analysis, and mediation analysis using Hayes’ PROCESS Macro Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples and 95% confidence intervals. The illustrative results suggested a positive association between AI-supported nutrition guidance and nutrition literacy (β = 0.463, R² = 0.214), alongside a positive relationship between AI-supported nutrition guidance and healthy dietary habits (r = 0.542). The illustrative mediation analysis indicated an indirect effect through nutrition literacy of 0.246, with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of [0.159, 0.343]. These numerical values are hypothetical and have not been calculated from actual participant responses. The study emphasizes that access to AI-generated nutrition information alone may not ensure healthier dietary decisions, as students must also be able to understand, evaluate, and apply the guidance they receive. Its proposed findings may inform university health education, digital nutrition literacy initiatives, and the development of more reliable AI-supported dietary resources. The research may also provide a foundation for future investigations into how digital nutrition guidance interacts with students’ knowledge, food choices, and everyday dietary practices. Longitudinal and experimental studies could further examine whether improvements in nutrition literacy are associated with sustained changes in healthy eating behaviors.

FinTech has shifted financial activity towards platforms that generate high-volume, high-velocity transaction data, creating new opportunities for fraud. This study examines the association between AI-enabled auditing and auditors' perceived fraud-detection effectiveness in FinTech environments, and whether this association varies with auditors' trust in AI tools. Drawing on trust-in-automation and technology acceptance research, we surveyed 214 auditors engaged with Iraqi banks and licensed electronic payment providers and tested the hypotheses using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped moderation analysis. The results show a positive association between AI-enabled auditing and perceived fraud-detection effectiveness. Auditor trust in AI has no statistically significant direct association with detection effectiveness, but it positively moderates the association between AI-enabled auditing and fraud detection: the estimated association is approximately 2.6 times stronger among high-trust auditors than among low-trust auditors. Trust therefore appears to act as a moderating condition rather than an independent predictor of perceived detection effectiveness. The study extends the discussion of audit technology beyond adoption to consider how trust conditions its perceived effectiveness. It also provides evidence from an emerging FinTech market in which research remains limited. For regulators, audit firms and FinTech supervisors, the findings suggest the importance of calibrated rather than uncritical trust in AI, supported by explainable tools, targeted training and clear guidance on AI-generated audit evidence.

Advanced Manufacturing (AM) is being transformed in an intelligent, adaptive, and data-driven production system with the help of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Data Analytics. This review discusses these technologies in improving the efficiency of processes, quality assurance and predictive decision making in major industries that include aerospace, automotive, biomedical and electronics. Such benefits as a massive decrease in defects, a high level of operational stability, and energy efficiency can be seen in real-world case studies that use AI-based digital twins, intelligent sensors, and autonomous control. Even with these developments, there are still issues with data quality, model transparency, cybersecurity and workforce preparedness. Future directions are also mentioned in the paper, such as generative AI, quantum-enabled optimization, and human-AI collaboration, which lead to sustainable and human-centric manufacture ecosystems of the Industry 5.0.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an essential tool in various fields, including journalism. However, the extent to which broadcast journalists in Taraba State, Nigeria embraced and utilized AI in their practices remains a subject of debate. It is on the above premise that this research examined Taraba State broadcast journalists' knowledge and usage of AI in journalistic practices. The paper was built on the technology acceptance model, diffusion of innovation theory, and social learning theory. The study adopted a qualitative approach where in-depth interviews were used. The in-depth interviews were conducted until the results reached saturation point. Findings of the study revealed that in journalists in Taraba State, Nigeria are slowly beginning to embrace AI for journalistic practice. However, there knowledge of AI usage for journalistic practices is low hence there is a significant knowledge gap that needs to be bridged. Therefore, the study recommends among other things that journalists in Taraba State need to gain more knowledge about AI and its potential applications in journalistic practices. The paper concludes that with proper training and guidance, journalists in Taraba State can harness the power of this AI technology to improve their reporting practices while ensuring ethical standards are upheld.

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in healthcare and education. Nursing students will enter AI-enabled clinical environments, yet evidence from Sri Lanka on their attitudes towards AI and how these relate to innovative behaviour is limited. This study assessed AI attitudes and innovative behaviour and examined their association among diploma nursing students in selected state nursing training schools in Sri Lanka. Methods A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 282 diploma nursing students from Kalutara and Galle Nursing Training Schools using systematic random sampling. Data were collected using an expert-reviewed and pretested self-administered questionnaire comprising sociodemographic items, the 13-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and the 10-item Innovative Work Behaviour Scale. Descriptive statistics and tests of normality were performed in IBM SPSS Statistics version 27. Because the total scores were not normally distributed, Spearman's rank-order correlation was used to examine the association between AI attitudes and innovative behaviour. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results Among 282 participants, 228 (80.9%) were female and 260 (92.2%) were third-year students. The mean AI attitude score was 44.32 (SD 4.65), and the mean innovative behaviour score was 35.73 (SD 4.79). AI attitude scores showed a weak but statistically significant positive correlation with innovative behaviour scores (Spearman's rho = 0.203, p < 0.001). Conclusions More favourable AI attitudes were associated with slightly higher innovative behaviour among diploma nursing students, although the association was weak and does not establish causality. The findings support consideration of structured, responsible AI literacy and innovation-focused learning activities in nursing education. Larger multi-site and longitudinal studies are needed to identify additional factors that shape innovative behaviour.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction Digital health training environments increasingly require scalable methods for assessing communication skills in realistic, interactive scenarios. This paper presents a comparative study of automated assessment approaches within a conversational AI virtual reality simulation designed for verbal de-escalation training. Methods A total of 20 nursing students completed the simulation, where their spoken responses were captured and converted to text through a speech-to-text system, and were evaluated across 11 de-escalation competencies. The evaluation compared three fine-tuned deep learning models (BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet) with a modified RATAS, a rubric-driven framework that leverages large language models. Two experiments were conducted: one using controlled 100-item validation datasets for each section, and another using the real-world responses collected during the user study. Results On the validation datasets, the deep learning models achieved the highest performance, with RoBERTa obtaining an average accuracy of 0.9927, followed by BERT at 0.9900 and XLNet at 0.9790, while RATAS achieved 0.8554. On the student-response dataset, performance decreased for all approaches, with RoBERTa obtaining 0.8590 accuracy, RATAS 0.8181, BERT 0.8000, and XLNet 0.7681. Discussion These results suggest that transformer-based models perform best under controlled conditions, whereas RATAS demonstrated stability in grading across different dataset types. These preliminary findings support the feasibility of integrating deep learning and rubric-driven LLM-based automated assessment approaches for communication and de-escalation training in nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: General Background The integration of Artificial Intelligence into public administration reshapes service delivery, data management, and bureaucratic decision-making processes. Specific Background While machine-driven operations optimize government services, they introduce complex legal challenges regarding system opacity, fragmented regulatory frameworks, and unclear liability when automated mechanisms intersect with societal interests. Knowledge Gap Existing studies predominantly emphasize digital transformation efficiency, leaving a critical void in addressing administrative liability and civic safeguards against systemic bias within fragmented domestic legal structures. Aims This study analyzes the adoption of automated technologies in state administration, focusing on establishing multi-layered liability and defending civic interests. Results Normative juridical analysis reveals that machine-driven administration requires a multi-layered supervisory architecture comprising mandatory human oversight, independent supervisory bodies, tiered sanctions, and the utilization of predictive analytics as an audit mechanism. Furthermore, defending citizens necessitates strict data privacy compliance, cybersecurity reinforcement, algorithmic transparency, equal digital access, and accessible legal remedies. Novelty This research adapts the risk supervision model from international frameworks into the domestic administrative legal system, bridging the current regulatory vacuum without necessitating entirely new statutory regimes. Implications Policymakers must implement adaptive risk guidelines and institutionalize explainable systems to ensure technological integration respects legal certainty, prevents prejudice, and maintains trust. Highlights Mandatory human oversight frameworks govern machine-driven decisions. Adapting international risk guidelines resolves domestic regulatory fragmentation. Transparent algorithmic processes coupled with cybersecurity protocols prevent systemic bias. Keywords Automated Innovation; Algorithmic Transparency; Risk Supervision; Data Privacy; Regulatory Fragmentation

Modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications use specialized models to perform different tasks.However, selecting a single model for all user queries may result in reduced performance when queries vary in intent and complexity.To overcome this challenge, this project proposes an "AutoML Framework for Intelligent Model Selection," a dynamic multi-agent system consisting of five specialized AI agents: Text Model,Embedding Model, Vision Model, Reasoning Model, and Code/Data Model.These agents collaboratively analyze incoming user queries and identify the most suitable model based on the requirements of each query.The framework incorporates an Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) evaluation engine using five algorithms: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and Naive Bayes.The system evaluates agent suitability using relevant query features and performance metrics, including Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves and Area Under the Curve (AUC) scores based on labelled evaluation data.The most suitable agent is selected to generate the final response.An interactive frontend dashboard displays agent scores, algorithmic metrics, selection results, and the reason behind the selected model.The proposed framework aims to provide intelligent, adaptive, and transparent model selection for different types of AI queries.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare and may improve efficiency in clinical support, health management, and doctor-patient communication. Yet its tendency to hallucinate, that is, to generate medical information that appears plausible but is false, can create systemic ethical risks in high-risk medical settings. This paper addresses two questions: what distinctive ethical risks are created by medical AI hallucinations, and what governance mechanisms can respond to them? Using the four principles of biomedical ethics as an analytical tool, the paper identifies four risk pathways: weakened informed consent, erosion of doctor-patient trust, harm to life and health, and unfair responsibility allocation. It then introduces responsible research and innovation (RRI) to build a four-dimensional framework of anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity, and responsiveness. The main contribution of the paper is to integrate biomedical ethical principles with RRI governance tools in the specific context of medical AI hallucinations, developing a closed-loop governance matrix across technology development, clinical application, and regulatory oversight. This provides an operational pathway for moving medical AI from technical feasibility towards ethical trustworthiness.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Although hospitals are introducing generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into documentation, messaging, and administrative workflows, model accuracy and time saved do not establish safe or sustainable implementation. This Mini Review examines which implementation and downstream outcomes should inform decisions to pilot, scale up, sustain, modify, or discontinue these workflows. A PubMed-led structured narrative search through 25 August 2026, with an update on 27 August, informed a purposive core of 17 empirical studies: seven direct administrative studies and 10 clinical-administrative studies. Supporting reviews and established implementation frameworks informed the interpretation of the findings. Perceived workload, logged efficiency, adoption, safety, and downstream outcomes did not improve consistently together. Favourable average quality could coexist with consequential errors and substantial verification work. Within this selected core, cost, penetration, and sustainability were measured less often than early fit, use, and feasibility. No study was coded as providing an operationalised equity assessment. We present a literature-informed outcome-to-decision crosswalk that links these findings to clinical workflow governance. This distinguishes non-compensable stop rules from minimum progression criteria and comparative value targets, with explicit ownership, denominators and reassessment. Illustrative stop rules address serious uncorrected errors, unauthorised data disclosure and bypassed human review. The crosswalk is an unvalidated normative synthesis, not a universal stage model. Its value requires prospective testing against patient safety, workforce burden and service outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of generating accurate, fluent, and personalized responses. Yet a response can be factually correct and still fail the person receiving it. Human questions arise within relationships, histories, emotional states, goals, uncertainties, and boundaries. The next stage of personalized AI therefore requires more than retrieval of user preferences or stylistic imitation. It requires a disciplined capacity to interpret the likely human context beneath an explicit request while preserving truth, agency, privacy, and the user’s authority to correct the system. This paper extends Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) by proposing a relational layer, described here as Relational-Emotional Synergy (RES), and a principle of constructive framing. RES treats meaning as something that can develop across an ongoing human-AI relationship rather than within isolated prompts alone. Constructive framing adds a directional obligation: when a user is discouraged, anxious, frustrated, or uncertain, the AI should not reflexively mirror negativity or offer unearned reassurance. It should acknowledge the circumstances honestly while, where appropriate, orienting the response toward clarity, realistic possibility, agency, and a useful next step. The paper deliberately remains text-centered. Voice, prosodic emotion sensing, and deeper multimodal inference are treated as future research rather than requirements of the present framework. It also recognizes language proficiency as an accessibility boundary: depth of thought should not be confused with fluency in written English or any dominant language. The central proposition is that personalized AI should seek to understand more deeply than the literal question asked, while never claiming certainty about a person’s inner state and never allowing personalization to outrun truth or human autonomy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Kazuo Ishiguro's Klara and the Sun (2021) has generally been read through the lens of posthumanism, with critics asking what the novel says about artificial minds, consciousness, and the ethical status of machines built to feel (Ajeesh and Rukmini; Sahu and Karmakar). Klara, the Artificial Friend (AF) who narrates the novel, is repeatedly framed by scholarship as a test case for whether a machine can possess genuine interiority, and whether human beings can ever truly know that interiority from the outside (Shang). This paper takes a different approach. Rather than asking what Klara is, it asks what Klara is used for. Read this way, Klara and the Sun is less a novel about artificial intelligence than a novel about human beings who cannot bear to look directly at loss, illness, and death, and who therefore route their most unbearable feelings through a listening, watching, uncomplaining object that will not look away, argue back, or die on its own schedule. Josie's mother, Chrissie, projects her anticipatory grief and her guilt over Josie's genetic "lifting" onto Klara by quietly preparing Klara to become a replacement daughter. Josie herself, isolated by illness from ordinary adolescent life, projects her need for an unthreatening companion onto Klara rather than risk further loss with human friends. Even Rick and the wider adult world around the Arthur family treat AFs as safe vessels for anxieties they will not name directly. Klara, in other words, functions across the novel as a screen: an entity human characters can fill with their own dread of mortality precisely because she seems not to have a mortality, or a claim, of her own.

Purpose Identifying exceptional leaders remains a top priority for organisations. Traditionally, leaders were selected using a battery of assessments measuring key personal attributes believed to make leaders successful. However, there has been a shift away from selecting leaders based on an a priori list of virtues, towards a focus on the actual behaviours linked to high performance. This abductive approach in competency framework development for leaders starts with the behaviours demonstrated in assessments and then constructs the competency framework in a bottom-up approach. Design/methodology/approach In the current study, a total of 15 411 leaders from 283 different companies and 38 countries completed a 3.5-hour online assessment centre simulation exercise. Natural language processing and machine learning were then utilised to identify 38 competencies by screening more than 30 million words. We then mapped this artificial intelligence-derived framework to prominent leadership models. Findings Despite strong congruence between frameworks, the abductive approach revealed three critical findings: 1) Not all competencies are equally distributed across the leader population; 2) Competencies are distributed across job levels, with some commonly observed in junior leadership roles and others primarily amongst senior leaders; and 3) the artefacts collected by the machine-learning algorithm enable a more granular view of the behaviours that constitute a competency compared to human assessors. Originality/value Using abductive methods to supplement deductive models capitalising on the strengths of both approaches, yield more nuanced leadership competency frameworks.

Abstract Single-cell transcriptome databases tell us which genes a cell type expresses, but what a cell type does, and what happens to it when a gene is perturbed, remains scattered across the literature. Cell IO (https://cell-io.riken.jp/) links these two kinds of knowledge through Cell Ontology identifiers. Its transcriptome layer re-processes 10x Chromium single- cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq experiments of human, mouse, and rat from the Sequence Read Archive with a uniform pipeline, annotates clusters with Cell Ontology terms restricted by the tissue of origin, and stores the cell type composition and UMAP embedding of every experiment (currently 14,931 experiments and 82.9 million cells). Its literature layer holds 895,258 claims extracted with a large language model and verified in a second pass from open-access abstracts, review articles, and gene perturbation studies in immunology and neuroscience, each with the verbatim sentence, highlighted entity spans, evidence strength, and ontology-normalized cell, gene, and context. The web interface lets users search cell types by name, synonym, or identifier, find the experiments in which a cell type is most abundant, inspect the composition and embedding of each experiment, read and filter the claims about a cell type by knowledge base, direction, evidence strength, and organism, and identify cell types whose functional characterization is missing from part of the literature. Cell IO is freely available without registration.

OBJECTIVES: To examine associations of changes in health literacy with subsequent changes in presenteeism and incident presenteeism among Japanese workers. METHODS: We analyzed 8 semiannual in-app surveys (June 2021-December 2024) from the DeSC database. Health literacy (HL) was measured with the 5-item Communicative and Critical Health Literacy scale (1-5), and presenteeism (Pres) with the WPAI-presenteeism item (0%-100%; higher indicating greater impairment; employed respondents only). Each observation used 3 consecutive waves: ΔHL(t-1)=HL(t-1)-HL(t-2) and subsequent ΔPres(t)=Pres(t)-Pres(t-1). Linear mixed models adjusted for prior Pres, earlier HL, and demographic, occupational, health-status, and lifestyle covariates; sensitivity analysis modeled prior Pres categorically. Additional analyses examined observations with prior presenteeism (Pres(t-1)>0), without prior presenteeism (Pres(t-1)=0) and categorical HL changes. RESULTS: Among 19,594 participants (60,203 observations), a 1-point more positive ΔHL was associated with more favorable subsequent ΔPres (β -1.24 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.52 to -0.97), with consistent sensitivity and prior-presenteeism findings; the incident odds ratio was 0.89 (0.84-0.93). Compared with unchanged HL, decreases were associated with less favorable changes (0.87; 0.46-1.27), whereas increases had a CI including zero (-0.32; -0.75 to 0.10). Increases of at least 0.6 points showed favorable exploratory associations. The individual-level association was modest (approximately -0.83 percentage points per standard deviation of ΔHL). CONCLUSIONS: More positive HL changes were associated with modestly more favorable presenteeism outcomes. Direction-based associations were clear for decreases but not increases; larger increases showed favorable exploratory associations. Intervention effects require further study.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Smart materials represent a rapidly advancing field in materials science, defined by their ability to respond dynamically to external stimuli such as temperature, pressure, light, electric and magnetic fields, and mechanical stress. To understand and optimize these behaviors, comprehensive characterization techniques are required that connect molecular-level processes with macroscopic performance. Stimuli–response mechanisms can be examined through spectroscopy, microscopy, and diffraction techniques, providing insight into structural and functional evolution. These techniques collectively support the characterization of diverse smart-material classes and have accelerated innovation across multiple disciplines. In biomedicine, force measurement and surface analysis inform the design of implants, sensors, and drug delivery systems. Despite this progress, challenges remain in standardizing and scaling characterization protocols and ensuring reproducibility across laboratories. Looking forward, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping characterization practices. AI-driven models can analyze large multimodal datasets from experimental techniques, uncovering patterns and correlations beyond conventional analysis. Integration of AI with experimental tools also enables more efficient interpretation of data and supports scalable material development. In conclusion, the characterization of smart materials forms the essential bridge between fundamental stimuli–response mechanisms and practical applications, guiding the rational design of next-generation smart materials.
