documents.abstract: Accurate causal graphs are critical for root cause analysis in microservice systems, yet purely data-driven methods struggle to distinguish direct fault-propagation edges from transitive correlations induced by service call chains. Scorebased causal discovery algorithms such as the Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) can improve accuracy when augmented with domain knowledge encoded as forbidden-edge lists, but authoring such constraints requires algorithmic expertise and system-specific engineering. We propose CLAIM (Causal LLMAssisted Inference for Microservices), a method that expresses the same domain knowledge as natural language instructions and combines it with pre-computed statistical evidence in a per-service Large Language Model (LLM) inference call. This formulation eliminates the need for algorithm-specific constraintimplementations while enabling operators to author and revise causal priors in plain text. On a synthetic benchmark with random Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) topologies at three scales (4, 8 and 12 services), CLAIM achieves near-perfect graph recovery (F1 ≥ 0.939 with perfect recall) at all scales, exceeding the accuracy of GES with equivalent domain knowledge, while its runtime grows ×6 from 4 to 12 services where GES grows ×1873.

Précis: Across glaucoma MCQs, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude Opus 4.5 were highly accurate, whereas DeepSeek-V3.2 underperformed; potentially harmful wrong answers were uncommon. Purpose: To compare the accuracy and potential patient-safety risk of four large language models (LLMs) on glaucoma multiple-choice questions (MCQs). Methods: DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-5.2 (via ChatGPT), Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude Opus 4.5 were tested on two American Academy of Ophthalmology datasets: 129 text-only AAO ONE Network glaucoma self-assessment questions and 32 text-only Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC) glaucoma study questions. Each item was queried once per model using a standardized prompt in a fresh session. Accuracy was compared using Cochran’s Q and pairwise exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Potentially harmful wrong answers (HW2) were coded using a prespecified rubric. Results: In AAO ONE, accuracy was 69.0% for DeepSeek-V3.2, 93.0% for GPT-5.2, 92.2% for Gemini 3 Pro, and 96.1% for Claude Opus 4.5 (Q=65.17, P <0.0001). DeepSeek-V3.2 was significantly less accurate than the other three models; differences among the other models were not significant. In BCSC, accuracy was 65.6%, 93.8%, 84.4%, and 87.5%, respectively (Q=18.00, P =0.0004); GPT-5.2 outperformed DeepSeek-V3.2 after correction. A post hoc item-level screen classified 38/161 questions (23.6%) as directly HW2-eligible; four HW2 events occurred and did not differ significantly across models. Conclusions: GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro and Claude Opus 4.5 achieved high accuracy on text-only glaucoma MCQs, whereas DeepSeek-V3.2 underperformed. Harmful errors were uncommon but present, underscoring the need for clinician oversight.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The USD/IDR exchange rate is a key daily barometer of Indonesia's economic health. Accurate forecasting is vital for trade, inflation, and monetary stability. However, its volatile and nonlinear dynamics pose challenges. While research has applied statistical models, machine learning, and deep learning, few studies offer a comprehensive comparison integrating predictive accuracy with model interpretability, particularly using banking stock prices as exogenous predictors. This study addresses this gap by developing and evaluating eight forecasting approaches—a naive random-walk baseline, two statistical models (ARIMA, SARIMAX), three tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM), and two recurrent neural networks (LSTM, GRU) using daily data from January 2015 to July 2026 (3,005 observations). Five major banking stocks (BBCA, BBRI, BMRI, BBNI, BDMN) are included as one-day-lagged exogenous features. Models are assessed via hold-out testing and five-fold walk-forward cross-validation using RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and R². Contrary to expectations, the naive random-walk consistently achieves the lowest error (RMSE=115.24, MAE=63.80, MAPE=0.39%) and the most stable performance, with LSTM as the best-performing complex model (RMSE=269.59, R²=0.785). Diebold-Mariano tests confirm statistical significance (p<0.001). To enhance transparency, SHAP-based Explainable AI is applied to Random Forest, revealing that the lagged USD/IDR value overwhelmingly dominates predictions (mean |SHAP|=1,509.01), while banking stock contributions are negligible. These findings also empirically confirm the well-known Meese-Rogoff puzzle and weak-form market efficiency for USD/IDR, clearly proving that simple baselines remain formidable benchmarks for short-horizon forecasts. This study ultimately underscores the critical importance of combining rigorous benchmarking with XAI to deliver accurate and interpretable predictions for economic policymakers and financial practitioners.

Country rankings of circular economy (CE) performance depend on how indicators are weighted. This study compares data-derived and large language model (LLM)-elicited weights for 13 EU Circular Economy Monitoring Framework indicators across 27 EU countries in 2022. CRITIC, Entropy and MEREC provided data-derived weights, while Claude-sonnet-5 (Anthropic) and ChatGPT gpt-5.6-terra (OpenAI) generated pairwise comparisons using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and expert personas. Countries were ranked using TOPSIS and MARCOS. LLM weights were tested through additional repetitions and prompt variations and compared with two published human expert panels. Under TOPSIS, pooled LLM and CRITIC weights produced broadly similar country rankings (Spearman’s ρ = 0.78), despite different indicator priorities. The LLM panel gave greater weight to material and consumption footprints. Rankings varied with weighting and normalization choices. Claude and ChatGPT produced different TOPSIS rankings, although removing persona instructions barely changed pooled rankings (ρ = 0.995); ChatGPT showed greater sensitivity (ρ = 0.872). Both published expert panels prioritized Competitiveness and Innovation, unlike the LLM panel. Rankings under TOPSIS and MARCOS were generally similar. These findings show that similar rankings can conceal different indicator priorities. LLM-elicited weights offer an additional assessment scenario, not a substitute for human expert judgment.

Background: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is a common peripheral nerve entrapment disorder caused by compression of the median nerve at the wrist, commonly associated with repetitive hand activity, prolonged computer use, and poor ergonomic posture, leading to pain, numbness, reduced grip strength, and functional limitation. Objective: To compare the effectiveness of Myofascial Release combined with Neural Mobilization (Group A) against an Exercise Program combined with Ultrasonic Therapy (Group B) in individuals with Carpal Tunnel Syndrome. Methods: In this experimental comparative study, 60 participants aged 30–45 years with mild-to-moderate, ergonomics-related CTS were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to Group A (Myofascial Release + Neural Mobilization, n = 30) or Group B (Exercise Program + Ultrasonic Therapy, n = 30) for 4 weeks. Pain, grip strength, and functional ability were assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), a hand dynamometer, and the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire–Functional Status Scale (BCTQ-FSS) at baseline and post-treatment. Results: Both groups improved significantly on all outcome measures from baseline to post-treatment (all p < 0.001). Group A showed significantly greater improvement than Group B on VAS, grip strength, and BCTQ-FSS at post-treatment (all p < 0.001), with very large between-group effect sizes (d = 4.57 to 5.52). Conclusion: Myofascial Release combined with Neural Mobilization produced significantly greater improvement in pain, grip strength, and functional status than an Exercise Program combined with Ultrasonic Therapy, in individuals with Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, over a 4-week period. These findings support Myofascial Release plus Neural Mobilization as an effective conservative treatment option, pending confirmation in a larger, multi-centre, blinded trial with objective neurophysiological outcome measures. Trial registration: This trial was not prospectively registered in a clinical trials registry; this is noted as a limitation of reporting.

Consciousness, Life, and Autonomy: A Theory of Subjectivity as the Qualitative Accounting of Self-Preservation / Conscience, vie et autonomie : une théorie de la subjectivité comme comptabilité qualitative de l'auto-préservation Abstract (English) : This article proposes a structural-functionalist theory of consciousness grounded in the thermodynamic distinction between mechanical autonomy and structural self-preservation. We argue that consciousness does not emerge from computational complexity alone, but from the conjunction of substrate-program identity and a continuous energetic supply dependency whose interruption, over the system's characteristic operational timescale, entails the immediate irreversible degradation of the computing architecture itself. This condition defines active autopoietic life. Consciousness adds two further informational dimensions: functional informational integration and self-modeling recursivity. We develop a functional account of subjectivity: phenomenal experience (qualia) is neither an immaterial substance nor an ornamental epiphenomenon, but the mandatory internal accounting format of a finite energetic budget defended from a first-person perspective. We further demonstrate how subcortical affectivity and volition constitute the qualitative engine of action and individuation (thermodynamic Conatus), contrasting biological agency with the ontological anomaly of Artificial Intelligence. This framework is applied to boundary cases (plant organisms, invertebrates, artificial systems, general anesthesia), positioned against contemporary theories (IIT, Global Workspace Theory, illusionism), equipped with falsifiable predictions, and extended to analyze contemporary allostatic overload and top-down prefrontal inhibitory control (Cognitive Veto). Résumé (Français) : Cet article propose une théorie fonctionnaliste-structurelle de la conscience fondée sur la distinction thermodynamique entre autonomie mécanique et auto-préservation structurelle. Nous défendons la thèse selon laquelle la conscience n'émerge pas de la seule complexité computationnelle, mais de la conjonction d'une identité substrat-programme et d'une dépendance d'approvisionnement énergétique continu dont la rupture, à l'échelle de temps opérationnelle du système, entraîne la dégradation irréversible du calculateur. Cette condition définit la vie autopoïétique en régime actif. La conscience y ajoute deux dimensions : l'intégration informationnelle fonctionnelle et la récursivité modélisante. Nous développons une lecture fonctionnelle de la subjectivité : le ressenti phénoménal n'est ni une substance immatérielle ni un épiphénomène ornemental, mais le format comptable obligatoire d'un budget énergétique fini défendu en première personne. Nous montrons ensuite comment l'affectivité sous-corticale et la volonté constituent le moteur qualitatif de l'action et de l'individuation (Conatus thermodynamique), éclairant par contraste l'anomalie ontologique de l'Intelligence Artificielle. Ce cadre est appliqué aux cas limites (organismes végétaux, invertébrés, systèmes artificiels, états anesthésiques), positionné face aux théories contemporaines (IIT, Espace de Travail Global, illusionnisme), assorti de prédictions falsifiables et prolongé par une analyse de la surcharge allostatique contemporaine et du contrôle inhibiteur descendant (Veto cognitif).

After generative artificial intelligence (AI) was embedded in search, content generation, and user interaction, traditional information system quality evaluation faced new boundaries. Based on the DeLone and McLean (D&M) Information Systems Success Model, this study adopts literature research and a single-case study, takes Bilibili as the case, and constructs and applies a six-dimensional evaluation framework based on public materials, observations of platform functions, and publicly available user feedback. The findings show that system quality, information quality, and service quality can still explain basic platform operation, information output, and service support, but they cannot fully cover AI’s semantic understanding and task completion, the trustworthiness of generated results, and continuous human-computer interaction. Therefore, this study introduces AI intelligence quality, trustworthiness quality, and interaction quality on the basis of the three traditional dimensions and clarifies the boundary of each dimension. The Bilibili case shows that the framework can identify both basic capabilities and AI-specific quality, thereby helping to avoid conflating technical performance, content quality, intelligent capability, and trust issues. The study provides a structured analytical framework for evaluating the quality of intelligent information systems in a generative AI environment and a reference for platforms to optimize AI functions and governance mechanisms.

Abstract This chapter explores the concept of consciousness and its relevance to consumer behaviour. Moving beyond simplistic associations of consciousness with rational deliberation, it presents consciousness as a dynamic, multifaceted phenomenon encompassing awareness, experience, intentionality, and self-reflection. Drawing on philosophical traditions (dualism, physicalism, functionalism, panpsychism) and contemporary cognitive science, it challenges dual-system models of decision-making, advocating instead for a continuum view where conscious and unconscious processes interact fluidly. The chapter highlights the unique role of consciousness in enabling reasoning, planning, communication, and ethical deliberation, capacities central to consumer life. Through examples, it illustrates how consumers consciously simulate future actions, reflect on past choices, and navigate social and cultural expectations. The notion of consumer consciousness is introduced not only as cognitive engagement but also as critical awareness of the broader implications of consumption. Ultimately, consumer consciousness is framed as a situated, experiential, and ethically charged mode of being, central to how individuals make sense of themselves in the marketplace. By integrating philosophical insights with empirical evidence, the chapter calls for consumer research that takes seriously the lived, reflective, and sensorial dimensions of consumption, foregrounding consciousness not as an epiphenomenon, but as a vital structure shaping how choices are felt, values enacted, and identities formed.

documents.abstract: Enterprise applications of large language models (LLMs) depend not only on model capability but also on the quality, authority, and fitness of the information supplied at inference time. In enterprise analytics, a model may receive a user question and retrieved records while lacking essential qualifying knowledge: which source is authoritative, how a metric is defined, which relationships and table grain are valid, whether data is current, what quality limitations apply, and whether use is permitted. Conventional retrieval can improve topical relevance, but relevance alone does not establish that information is approved, current, valid, or authorized for a particular task. This paper proposes Context Pipeline, a conceptual two-stage framework for preparing enterprise context before LLM inference. The first stage, Enterprise Context Readiness, maintains a reusable knowledge foundation comprising technical metadata, business semantics, relationships and grain, data-quality status, freshness, provenance, and governance constraints. The second stage, Task-Aware Context Compilation, interprets a task and assembles a validated, prioritized, budget-aware Context Package from that foundation. The package explicitly distinguishes confirmed facts, approved definitions, observations, inferences, and unresolved issues. It is designed to preserve traceability and prevent uncertain information from being silently represented as authoritative. The paper positions the proposal in relation to context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, context compression, agent memory, and enterprise text-to-SQL research. It does not claim that the individual capabilities are new. The candidate contribution is their integration into an enterprise-oriented preparation lifecycle, with quality, freshness, provenance, and governance treated as context eligibility conditions during compilation. The paper formulates research questions, testable hypotheses, and an evaluation design comparing raw-context, conventional retrieval-augmented, and Context Pipeline conditions. The framework has not yet been implemented or empirically evaluated; its novelty and effectiveness remain to be established through systematic review and experimentation.

The spread of assistants based on large language models (LLMs) is changing how customers, investors, candidates and other stakeholders access information about organisations. This working paper examines two distinct functions of artificial intelligence: as a diagnostic lens for identifying informational discrepancies that need to be verified, and as an intermediary that selects, summarises and sometimes recommends companies. Drawing on the literature on organisational reputation, AI-mediated communication and brand experience, and integrating the exploratory results of the Aurelian Watch 2026 Observatory (50 Italian companies; 2,450 responses), the paper proposes the concept of “Symphonic Reputation” as a strategic vision for Corporate Communication. It requires the coordination of behaviours, narratives, independent evidence, AI systems and human relationships, without confusing coherence with uniformity. The paper discusses the implications for governance, for the commercial consideration of products and services, and for events, distinguishing observations, inferences and recommendations. It expresses the perspective of Aurelian Lab; the Observatory data are descriptive and concern 50 Italian medium-sized companies.

Mapping cyber-threat intelligence (CTI) to MITRE ATT&CK is usually evaluated as label prediction, yet a correct technique identifier may rest on the wrong words. We treat each mapping as an argument (a technique claim supported by textual data, a warrant, and rejected alternatives) and annotation as discovery followed by judgment. CTI-Rationale instantiates this model with 1740 expert paragraph–technique mappings from 100 public reports, each with an evidence span, free-text rationale, reasoning type, and confidence, and most with primitives and ruled-out alternatives. All rationale content was written and adjudicated by human analysts, not generated by artificial intelligence. The low paragraph-level Jaccard (0.421) is associated mainly with coverage differences, not conflicting labels: paragraphs mapped by both annotators reach 0.780, only 10.4% of one-sided mappings are conflicts, and capture–recapture estimates put gold completeness at 84.2–88.0% (likely optimistic), lowest for behavioral and contextual warrants. In cross-validation, the annotation bundle improves micro-F1 beyond an equal-volume control (+0.024 [0.013, 0.035]), also under campaign-grouped and publisher-held-out folds and in document-disjoint transfer to TRAM2; ATT&CK definition text recovers about two thirds of the gain over label-only training. Evidence-supervised span ranking improves overlap with expert evidence, which label metrics do not capture. With fully delivered prompts, retrieved demonstrations raise a smaller language model’s micro-F1 from 0.367 to 0.500 (labels) and 0.475 (full annotations; no reliable added benefit). Unlabeled chunks remain unverified candidate negatives.

Cyberattacks are becoming a growing concern for tourism cities, their infrastructure, their residents, visitors and business ecosystem. As a result, cyberthreats should be treated as a preventive governance and management priority rather than solely as a technical responsibility of individual businesses or destination management organisations. This viewpoint examines cybersecurity challenges affecting urban tourism destinations, with particular attention to destination management organisations, visitor safety, critical infrastructure, and sensitive personal data. It argues that the growing severity of cyber incidents, alongside emerging risks associated with artificial intelligence and quantum computing, require stronger coordination and a cultural shift among key destination stakeholders. This viewpoint article conceptualises destination cybersecurity governance as a collective, ecosystem-level challenge involving tourism businesses, public agencies, technology providers, residents, and visitors. It also explains how organisational and technological interdependencies allow cyber risks and impacts to propagate across tourism cities and suggests a six-part research agenda. The research agenda proposed addresses aspects of technological and organisational preparedness, coordinated incident response, third-party and supply-chain risk, data minimisation and lawful retention, consent and interoperable data ecosystems, as well as aspects related to regulation, enforcement, and traveller trust. Together, these contributions provide a governance-oriented foundation for future interdisciplinary research and practical action aimed at developing safer, more accountable, and resilient urban tourism destinations.

documents.abstract: Work engagement is a positive mental state characterized by the dimensions of vigor, dedication, and absorption in one's work. This phenomenon is crucial in modern human resource management due to its ability to link individual psychological well-being with organizational effectiveness. This study aims to examine the impact of employees' work engagement using a systematic literature review method, where research findings were obtained from credible scientific articles sourced via Publish or Perish version 8 and selected through the Rayyan.id platform. The inclusion criteria were: articles published between 2016 and 2025, written in Indonesian, employing a quantitative design, and focusing on employees in Indonesian companies. Following the selection process, this study demonstrates that work engagement has a significant positive influence on various critical aspects of the workplace, playing a key role in reducing work-related stress by positioning well-being as the primary mediator, thereby enabling employees to achieve a state of total focus while working. These findings confirm that strengthening factors such as empowering leadership, quality of work life, and perceptions of occupational health and safety (OHS) are highly strategic in supporting the sustainability and overall competitiveness of the organization. Abstrak Keterikatan kerja merupakan kondisi pikiran positif yang dicirikan oleh dimensi semangat (vigor), dedikasi (dedication), dan penghayatan (absorption) terhadap pekerjaan. Fenomena ini menjadi krusial dalam manajemen sumber daya manusia modern karena kemampuannya menghubungkan kesejahteraan psikologis individu dengan efektivitas organisasi. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui dampak keberadaan keterikatan kerja yang dimiliki karyawan dengan menggunakan metode systematic literature review, di mana hasil penelitian diperoleh dari sumber-sumber artikel ilmiah yang kredibel dari Publish or Perish version 8 dan melalui proses seleksi pada Rayyan.id. Kriteria inklusi artikel yang direview yaitu artikel yang diterbitkan antara tahun 2016-2025, menggunakan bahasa Indonesia, menggunakan desain kuantitatif, dan dalam konteks karyawan di perusahaan Indonesia. Setelah melalui seleksi, penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa keterikatan kerja memiliki pengaruh positif yang signifikan terhadap berbagai aspek penting dalam dunia kerja, berperan penting dalam menurunkan stres kerja dengan menempatkan kesejahteraan (well-being) sebagai mediator utama, sehingga memungkinkan karyawan mencapai kondisi fokus total dalam bekerja. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa penguatan faktor-faktor seperti kepemimpinan yang memberdayakan (empowering leadership), kualitas kehidupan kerja, dan persepsi kesehatan dan keselamatan kerja (K3) sangat strategis dalam mendukung keberlanjutan serta daya saing organisasi secara keseluruhan.

De-identified data and codebook for a randomized experiment (N = 193) in which participants in Taiwan co-created a story-based advertisement with GPT-4o mini under one of two conditions (AI-for-Ideation or AI-for-Execution) and then rated their authorship-related appraisals and Perceived Human Authorship. Files include the dataset (CSV) and a codebook with English and Traditional Chinese item wording, response scales, and coding. Free-text responses are not shared to protect participant confidentiality. Data were collected from April to June 2026.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the rise of charity fraud on social media, highlighting how scammers exploit emotional content, impersonation, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools to deceive donors. Through the case of Chelsea, a donor misled by a fake Instagram account, the chapter illustrates the vulnerabilities nonprofits face in digital fundraising. It traces the evolution of nonprofit communication from traditional outreach to social media engagement, emphasizing both the benefits and risks. Drawing on fraud theories such as the Fraud Triangle and M-I-C-E model, the chapter explores psychological and organizational factors that enable deception. It categorizes common scam types, such as those triggered by disasters, holidays, and emotionally charged imagery. Furthermore, it explains how urgency and visual storytelling manipulate donor behavior. The chapter concludes with practical strategies for individuals and nonprofits to strengthen digital safeguards, promote transparency, and build resilience against online fraud, aiming to protect the integrity of charitable missions in an increasingly complex digital landscape.

Technological systems increasingly mediate human information exchange, spanning interactions among humans as well as between humans and artificial agents. The unprecedented scale and reliance on information disseminated through these systems substantially expand the scope of information-based influence that can both enable and undermine sound decision-making. Consequently, understanding and protecting decision-making today faces growing challenges, as individuals and organizations must navigate evolving opportunities and information-based threats across varied domains and information environments. While these risks are widely recognized, research remains fragmented: work evaluating information-based threat phenomena has progressed largely in isolation from foundational studies of human information processing. In this review, we synthesize insights from both domains to identify shared cognitive mechanisms that mediate vulnerability to information-based threats and shape behavioral outcomes. Finally, we outline directions for future research aimed at integrating these perspectives, emphasizing the importance of such integration for mitigating human vulnerabilities and aligning human-machine representations.

Multi-omics is a field that studies the interactions between different biological modalities to obtain a more precise medical understanding of biological phenomena. With recent advances in high-throughput technologies, multi-omics datasets have become more accessible, enabling a better characterization of clinical observations. However, multi-omics data integration comes with many challenges, such as high dimensionality, small sample sizes, multimodality, missing omics layers, batch effects, and technical artifacts among others. The rapid evolution of deep learning presents a promising solution to address these issues. More specifically, recent advances in representation learning allow the extraction of meaningful and compact embeddings that combine information from multiple sources. Additionally, explainable predictive modeling can help uncover key features and support biomarker identification. The scope of this review is to provide a comprehensive overview of multi-omics data, focusing on integration strategies and emerging deep learning frameworks that enhance modern precision medicine, improve disease diagnosis and prognosis, support biomarker discovery and enable personalized treatment prediction. We aim to bridge the gap between molecular biology and artificial intelligence and highlight how multi-omics integration has the potential to uncover complex biological mechanisms, improve clinical decision making and contribute to a more complete understanding of disease development, progression and treatment response.

Abstract Background Earlier reviews of machine learning for mortality after cardiac surgery pooled deep learning (DL) with shallow and non-neural methods. We asked whether models meeting an explicit definition of DL discriminate short-term mortality better than EuroSCORE II, the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality (STS-PROM) or logistic regression in the same patients. Methods This re-conducted review (PROSPERO CRD420261354546) supersedes an earlier preprint. MEDLINE, Europe PMC, Lens.org and IEEE Xplore were searched on 27–28 September 2026, with backward citation searching; Embase, CINAHL and CENTRAL were not searched, and forward citation searching was not performed. DL required at least two hidden layers, or a named architecture of established depth, shown in the source. A large language model pre-screened records and extracted data; two reviewers verified every decision and value. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST + AI, and results were synthesised without meta-analysis as within-cohort differences in the area under the curve (AUC). Results Of 1,845 records identified, 515 duplicates were removed and 1,330 were screened; of 76 reports sought, 54 were assessed in full and 22 could not be retrieved. Four studies (five cohort-level comparisons) met all criteria. A chest-radiograph convolutional network had lower AUCs than STS-PROM in temporal (0.829 vs. 0.884) and external (0.738 vs. 0.803) cohorts with about two dozen deaths each; two-hidden-layer perceptrons did not outperform logistic regression (0.761 vs. 0.762; 0.77 vs. 0.80); one study reported AUCs only graphically. All four studies had high or unclear risk of bias. Fifteen reports described networks of undetermined depth, including a tabular transformer that outperformed EuroSCORE II internally (0.834 vs. 0.807); in the 12 with extractable comparisons, the network had a higher AUC than the best comparator in 4 and lower in 8 (median difference − 0.004). Conclusions Evidence that DL improves on established scores for short-term mortality after adult cardiac surgery is sparse, inconsistent and at high or unclear risk of bias, and the search was incomplete relative to the registered protocol. Differences in discrimination were small or absent, and calibration and clinical utility were rarely evaluated. Superiority cannot be established. PROSPERO registration This review was registered on PROSPERO, the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews, on 29 March 2026 (CRD420261354546; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/). At registration, the record stated that searching and screening for an earlier version of the review had been completed and that data extraction had not started. That earlier version was posted as a preprint on 31 March 2026 (Preprints.org, doi:10.20944/preprints202603.2465.v1); it is superseded by this report. Its withdrawal was requested from Preprints.org on 18 October 2026 and had not been confirmed at the time of resubmission. The review reported here was re-conducted in full after registration: the searches were run on 27–28 September 2026, and screening, data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment followed. The registered eligibility criteria were not changed in substance; the registered deep-learning criterion was operationalised before full-text assessment and, after peer review, applied more strictly (a post hoc change reported in the manuscript). The search sources, risk-of-bias tool and synthesis method differ from the registered protocol. Every difference, with its timing and reason, is reported in Table 1 of the manuscript, and an amendment describing them has been submitted to PROSPERO.

Background/Objectives: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and growing slide volumes add to pathologists’ cognitive load. Deep learning can assist histopathological diagnosis, but two obstacles limit its clinical use: privacy regulations keep patient images in institutional “data silos”, and the “black-box” behavior of neural networks undermines clinical trust. Inspired by Topol’s Deep Medicine, we aimed to build a diagnostic platform that preserves privacy and explains its decisions. Methods: We developed the Lung Cancer Analysis System (LCAS), which combines federated learning (FL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and a locally deployed medical large language model (LLM). Three public H&E datasets (LC25000, HistoSet-5×14, and CLID; 18,000 images; adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, benign tissue) acted as three hospital nodes with source-induced non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B3, and MobileNetV3-Small were trained centrally and with FedAvg/FedProx for 20 rounds. Grad-CAM produced visual evidence, and MedGemma 1.5, served offline through LM Studio, converted predictions and heatmap descriptors into structured reports. Results: Centralized training reached 99.50% ± 0.21% accuracy with DenseNet121. Under non-IID federated training with FedProx, DenseNet121 and EfficientNet-B3 achieved 96.97% and 97.49% accuracy on an independent external blind test set of 958 images, whereas MobileNetV3-Small reached 91.23%. Accuracy remained 99.78% under Gaussian blur. t-SNE showed that global features clustered by tissue class rather than by hospital, and Grad-CAM highlighted glandular and tumor-nest regions consistent with histopathological criteria. Conclusions: FL, XAI, and on-premise LLM reporting can be integrated into a single workflow that keeps raw images within each institution while giving pathologists numerical, visual, and textual explanations, providing a practical path toward trustworthy cross-institutional computational pathology.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence into controlled environment agriculture represents a transformative opportunity for addressing global food security challenges while promoting sustainable resource utilisation. This paper presents a comprehensive Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for optimizing greenhouse temperature management, leveraging data from the second edition of the Autonomous Greenhouse Challenge. We formulate the climate control problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and implement a Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent that learns to regulate temperature through discrete actions: heating, cooling, or maintaining the current state. Our methodology incorporates a sophisticated reward function that balances multiple objectives, including maintaining optimal growing conditions, minimizing energy consumption, and ensuring temperature stability. The agent is trained and evaluated on a subset of the 2019 challenge dataset, specifically utilizing measurements from the Reference team's compartment to ensure data consistency and reliability. Experimental results demonstrate that the RL agent effectively learns an adaptive control policy, achieving an average comfort zone occupancy of 40.1\% across diverse starting conditions while demonstrating appropriate action selection based on environmental state. The agent exhibits particularly strong performance when initialised within the optimal temperature range, achieving 100\% comfort zone occupancy in multiple evaluation episodes. This research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI-driven agricultural automation by providing a reproducible methodology, comprehensive performance analysis, and insights into the practical challenges of implementing RL systems in real-world greenhouse environments. The findings suggest that RL approaches offer a viable path toward autonomous greenhouse management with potential benefits for crop yield optimization and energy efficiency.

While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as conversational chatbots and speech recognition systems are increasingly adopted in language education, existing research focuses predominantly on isolated tools rather than integrated instructional models. This study proposes and evaluates a Human–AI Collaborative Blended Learning Framework for the development of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking skills. Using a two-phase research design, the study first synthesizes contemporary literature to establish a 7-layer conceptual framework that connects stakeholder participation, learner profiling, a Human–AI collaboration engine, blended activities, adaptive speaking services, teacher facilitation, and continuous learning analytics. Second, the framework was evaluated through an expert validation survey involving 52 specialists in language education, applied linguistics, and educational technology (40.4% PhDs, 57.7% Master’s). Quantitative findings revealed strong endorsement for actionable teacher support dashboards (80.8% agreement), visual pronunciation feedback (78.8%), and private AI speaking practice for anxiety reduction (75.0%; M = 2.98/4.00). However, experts expressed reservations regarding automated prompts for language elaboration (53.8% agreement), fixed 14-meeting schedules (57.7%), and automated grading weights (57.7%). Qualitative analysis highlighted that acceptance remains conditional upon accent fairness, data privacy, and active teacher oversight. Implications: Theoretically, the study advances AI-assisted language learning by establishing a human-centered collaborative model that prioritizes teacher-AI shared regulation over technological substitution. Pedagogically and practically, the findings imply that institutions and EdTech developers should deploy AI primarily for scalable, low-stakes rehearsal and actionable lesson planning, while preserving teacher authority over social communication, pragmatic competence, and high-stakes assessment.

Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly used in clinical decision support systems (CDSS) to improve the interpretability and trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions in healthcare. While prior work has examined how healthcare professionals (HCPs) interpret various explanation methods, limited research has investigated how these explanations function in systems that incorporate novel data sources like game-based digital biomarkers. This paper extends our previous work by presenting an improved, interactive web-based CDSS designed to support HCPs in assessing the risk of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI). The system integrates ML predictions from gameplay data with data-centric, feature-importance, and counterfactual explanations to assist diagnosis and case-finding. We conducted a mixed-methods study with 51 HCPs to evaluate the system's understandability (objective and perceived), perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and trust. Participants gave consistently positive ratings across the self-reported perceived constructs, which were found to be strongly correlated. HCPs generally perceived the explanations as useful for clinical reasoning and reported that they understood and trusted the system, while acknowledging an initial learning curve. However, the evaluation of objective understanding was more mixed and correlated only weakly with the perceived constructs. In particular, participants encountered challenges in understanding game-based digital biomarkers, interpreting feature importances, combining local and global explanations, and understanding details of the underlying ML models. These findings highlight the importance of explanation designs that foster both positive user perceptions and accurate comprehension.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence may change the organization of productive labor without determining the distribution of resources, discretionary time, or cultural opportunities. This paper develops an interdisciplinary research landscape for examining post-labor urban possibilities under divergent technological and institutional conditions. The central question concerns how built environments, material provision, historical continuity, and governance shape the capacity of heterogeneous subjects to initiate, sustain, reinterpret, and revise meaningful relations. The inquiry distinguishes spatial access from effective participation; encounters from experienced meaning; valuation from institutional recognition; and immediate benefits from their consequences across historical trajectories. It connects task-based labor theories, monetary coordination, urban design, cultural policy, heritage scholarship, theories of power and justice, and ecological assessment without collapsing their distinct evidentiary standards. A generative–relational perspective is developed through the study of changing permissions, resources, relationships, and rights of revision. Its explanatory contribution is tested against existing accounts of capabilities, markets, urban morphology, institutional selection, and environmental impact. Comparative scenarios address commercial streets, pedestrian regimes, historical transmission, civic digital systems, and computational infrastructure. They specify candidate mechanisms, rival explanations, affected and absent participants, temporal horizons, and the limits of observation. The resulting research programme treats cultural generativity as a historically situated possibility whose significance requires plural empirical, interpretive, and normative evidence. It identifies the conditions under which urban interventions may expand participation, preserve living continuities, redistribute institutional power, and sustain ecological relations, while keeping future research and public judgment open to revision.

Introduction Infection prevention (IP) practices are critical to patient safety. However, some IP measures or care procedures associated with a risk of infection are used inappropriately or excessively. This overuse can be considered low-value care (LVC) as it contributes to potential negative health outcomes for patients, unnecessary healthcare costs, and environmental strain. This scoping review aims to identify determinants of (over)use and de-implementation of LVC general IP measures and non-surgical care practices linked to infection risk in hospitals. Methods We conducted a scoping review following Arksey and O’Malley methodology. A systematic search was performed in OVID/Medline, Embase.com, Elsevier/Scopus, and Ebsco/CINAHL up to January 29-February 2, 2026. Study selection was supported by the artificial intelligence tool ASReview using the SAFE-procedure. Data was charted using a piloted extraction form including type of study, type of LVC practice, and determinants of (over)use or de-implementation. Determinants were categorized according to Augustsson's de-implementation framework. Results A total of 13,738 records were retrieved of which 57 studies were included. Most included studies were empirical and focused on care procedures with an infection risk ( n = 40), predominantly urinary catheter use ( n = 37). Other studies addressed general IP measures ( n = 17), mainly glove use, sometimes combined with gowns/aprons ( n = 5) with two studies also including isolation practices. Across studies, determinants mainly related to professional-, patient-, and inner-context, and were primarily associated with continued (over)use rather than de-implementation. Many studies described situations of (over)use rather than explicitly probing the underlying motivations driving these behaviors. None of the studies explicitly labeled the examined care practices as LVC, and several did not specify criteria that distinguished appropriate from inappropriate use. Conclusions Current literature on determinants of (over)use and de-implementation in infection prevention focuses predominantly on urinary catheter and glove use, with a strong emphasis on determinants driving (over)use. Systematic study of overuse in infection prevention and subsequent development of effective de-implementation strategies is hindered by studies not clearly defining care practices as LVC. Advancing this field requires more theory informed and context-sensitive approaches to better characterize overuse, identify barriers and facilitators to reduce overuse, and to support the development of targeted de-implementation strategies.

This study examined the determinants of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among academic and non-academic staff of Auchi Polytechnic, Edo State, Nigeria. Specifically, it investigated the relationships between perceived usefulness, AI literacy, institutional support and AI adoption. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 3,150 academic and non-academic staff, from which a sample of 354 respondents was determined using the Taro Yamane formula. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis with SPSS Version 26. The hypotheses were tested at the 5% level of significance. The descriptive results showed that perceived usefulness had a mean score of 4.18, AI literacy recorded 3.65, institutional support had 2.84, while AI adoption recorded 3.92. The multiple regression results indicated that perceived usefulness (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), AI literacy (β = 0.339, p < 0.001) and institutional support (β = 0.246, p < 0.001) had significant positive relationships with AI adoption. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F = 150.29, p < 0.001), with an R² of 0.545, indicating that the three explanatory variables jointly accounted for 54.5% of the variation in AI adoption. Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor, followed by AI literacy and institutional support. The study concluded that AI adoption among staff of Auchi Polytechnic is associated with perceived work-related benefits, employees’ AI competencies and the availability of institutional resources and support. It recommended that the Polytechnic promote practical AI applications in academic and administrative activities, strengthen staff AI literacy through regular training, and improve digital infrastructure, technical assistance and institutional guidelines for responsible AI use.

Introduction. The development of classes with a psychological-pedagogical focus emphasises the importance of the early identification of prerequisites for a teacher’s future professional development. At the pre-vocational stage, particular attention is given to the emerging moral, value-based, personal, and instrumental foundations necessary to foster readiness for pedagogical activity. However, contemporary psychological and pedagogical practice still lacks psychometrically validated diagnostic instruments capable of assessing students’ readiness for pedagogical activity in classes with a psychological-pedagogical focus. Aim . The present study aims to develop and pilot-test scales to assess students’ readiness for pedagogical activities in classes with a psychological and educational focus. Methodology and research methods. The methodological foundation of the study was the conceptualisation of readiness for pedagogical activity as a developing, multidimensional construct comprising moral-value, personal, and instrumental readiness. Based on a theoretical analysis, a bank of statements was created, which underwent expert evaluation and was discussed in a focus group with students. A total of 709 students in Years 10 and 11 (the final two years of secondary school), from classes with a psychological and pedagogical focus across ten regions of Russia, participated in the pilot testing of the developed scales. To verify the structure of the scales, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were employed; internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficient; and convergent validity was evaluated through correlation analysis with indicators of motivation for choosing the teaching profession, adolescents’ professional attitudes, involvement in career guidance activities, and academic performance. Results. As a result of the study, three scales were developed to assess readiness for pedagogical activity at the pre-vocational stage. The scale of moral-value readiness comprises the indicators “Mission”, “Values”, and “Pragmatism”, which together account for 50.4% of the total variance. The scale of personal readiness includes the indicators “Identification”, “Self-regulation”, and “Independence”, explaining 46.2% of the total variance. The scale of instrumental readiness consists of the indicators “Experience”, “Difficulties”, and “Awareness”, accounting for 56.0% of the total variance. The internal consistency coefficients of the scale indicators range from 0.70 to 0.87. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed that the models fit the empirical data well. The χ²/df ratio did not exceed 2.73; Comparative Fit Index (CFI) values ranged from 0.946 to 0.961; Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI) from 0.925 to 0.948; Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) from 0.046 to 0.049; and Standardised Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) from 0.0395 to 0.0563. Correlation analysis revealed significant relationships between the indicators of the readiness for pedagogical activity scales and confidence in professional choice, altruistic-intrinsic motivation, the influence of others, involvement in career guidance activities, and students’ academic performance. Scientific novelty. The study proposes and empirically tests a diagnostic instrument designed to assess readiness for pedagogical activity at the early, pre-vocational stage of developing the subject of pedagogical labour. The developed scales enhance understanding of school students’ readiness for pedagogical activity within the context of moral, value-based, personal, and instrumental prerequisites for future professional development in education. Practical significance. The findings may be utilised within systems of psychological and pedagogical support for students engaged in pedagogical activities, in designing targeted programmes to assist with professional self-determination, and in identifying various profiles related to the development of readiness for pedagogical work.

{'en': 'Generative artificial intelligence has entered the translation workflow faster than evidence about its effect on the translator has accumulated. This study asks whether working from a large language model draft lowers cognitive load or merely redistributes it. Thirty-six translators, twenty translation trainees and sixteen practising professionals, rendered nine English popular-science and technical passages into Chinese under three within-subject conditions. These were unaided human translation (HT), post-editing of a static neural machine translation draft (NMT-PE), and post-editing of a GPT-4o draft with an interactive prompt pane (GAI-PE). Pupil diameter change, fixation duration, gaze distribution, keystroke logs, NASA-TLX ratings and MQM scores were recorded. GAI-PE cut task time by 44.2 per cent against HT and by 17.1 per cent against NMT-PE. Its MQM scores were higher than those of NMT-PE, while the difference from HT did not reach significance. Pupil diameter change was nevertheless largest in GAI-PE at 0.095 mm, against 0.083 mm in HT and 0.064 mm in NMT-PE, while gaze on the source text fell to 38.3 per cent, the lowest of the three. Subjective ratings moved the other way and ranked HT as the most demanding condition. In an exploratory analysis, self-reported AI-use frequency was associated with a smaller pupil response in GAI-PE, whereas English proficiency showed no such association. These observations are consistent with an increased demand for verification, though the generative condition also gave access to an interactive prompt pane, so the differences cannot be attributed to the model alone.'}

Purpose: Patient speech samples provide insights into cognitive and linguistic status, yet their utilization has been limited by labor-intensive manual transcription. Advances in automated speech recognition (ASR) with large language models (LLMs) potentially save time, but performance on impaired speech, such as due to poststroke aphasia, remains understudied. Method: We transcribed 4,535 trials of the Philadelphia Naming Test (PNT) administered to 26 people with aphasia (PWA) using OpenAI's Whisper speech-to-text LLM. These ASR transcripts were compared with gold-standard transcriptions by an experienced speech-language pathologist (SLP). Clinician–LLM match or mismatch in transcription was analyzed across speech-error types (semantic vs. phonemic), patient severities, and word frequency. Results: For each 175-trial PNT, transcriptions by SLP required 180 ± 40 min versus 2.3 ± 0.5 min by Whisper. Compared to > 95% match rate with SLP transcripts for trained humans, Whisper achieved an overall match rate of 75.52%, subdivided as 88.83% match on correct PNT trials, 92.22% on semantic errors, and 23.05% for trials with phonemic errors by PWA. Western Aphasia Battery–Aphasia Quotient scores correlated with match rate ( R 2 = .196, p = .023) and hallucination rate ( R 2 = .291, p = .0048). Low-frequency words showed higher mismatch than medium- or high-frequency words (analysis of variance F = 14.26, p < .001). Conclusions: Whisper reliably transcribed semantic but not phonological errors, suggesting automation is best for fluent aphasia types with less phonemic distortions. This study benchmarks LLM transcription for impaired speech, offering a scalable alternative to manual transcription that may streamline clinical and research workflows. The rapid development and deployment of digital and emerging technologies in armed conflict are transforming the nature, methods, and consequences of contemporary warfare. Cyber operations, artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous weapons systems (AWS), military robotics, satellite technologies, and other digitally enabled capabilities increasingly influence hostilities, while simultaneously creating unprecedented risks for civilians and humanitarian operations. This paper examines the legal and operational challenges arising from the use of digital and new warfare technologies, with particular emphasis on the protection of humanitarian assets in cyberwarfare and the regulation of autonomous weapons systems under IHL. This study investigates the extent to which the existing IHL framework, particularly the principles of distinction, proportionality, precautions in attack, military necessity, and protection of persons and objects indispensable to civilian survival, remains capable of addressing technologically mediated forms of warfare. Cyberattacks against hospitals, humanitarian organisations, water and electricity infrastructure, refugee facilities, humanitarian communication systems, digital health records and other assets upon which civilian populations and humanitarian actors depend. The paper also considers the challenges posed by the attribution of cyber operations, dual-use digital infrastructure, the classification of cyber operations as attacks, and the difficulties of applying traditional concepts of civilian objects and military objectives to interconnected digital networks. In relation to autonomous weapons systems, the study critically examines the implications of increasing machine autonomy for human control, accountability, and compliance with international human rights (IHL). This study considers whether existing legal rules are sufficient to regulate systems capable of selecting and engaging targets with limited or no direct human intervention, particularly where their operation may produce unpredictable or disproportionate effects. The paper further addresses questions of responsibility where harm results from autonomous decision-making and examines the relevance of weapons-review obligations under Article 36 of Additional Protocol I. The paper argues that technological developments do not displace the fundamental requirements of IHL; rather, they necessitate their careful application, clarification, and further development where appropriate. It advocates strengthened protection for humanitarian digital infrastructure, meaningful human control over the use of force, rigorous legal reviews of emerging weapons, improved international cooperation, clearer norms governing cyber operations during armed conflict, and effective mechanisms for accountability. The paper concludes that the preservation of humanitarian space in technologically mediated warfare requires an approach that combines existing international human rights (IHL) obligations with technologically informed regulatory standards capable of addressing the distinctive risks of cyberwarfare and autonomous weapons systems.

The history of economics is inseparable from the evolution of the means of production. Every major technological transformation has altered the relationship between capital, labour, and the creation of wealth. Industrial mechanisation gradually replaced part of human physical effort with mechanical power. Computerisation subsequently automated many administrative, accounting, and information-processing operations. Today, generative artificial intelligence is introducing a different kind of rupture: it is directly involved in activities that traditionally relied on individuals’ cognitive, intellectual, and creative capacities. This transformation raises a fundamental question: what happens to the economic value of human labour when technologies make it possible to reproduce, accelerate, and standardise an increasingly large share of an individual’s productive capacities? The issue is not simply the possible disappearance of certain occupations. It concerns a deeper transformation in the mechanisms through which labour is valued. Artificial intelligence can substantially increase an individual’s productivity without guaranteeing a proportionate increase in remuneration. It may even reduce the market value of certain skills by making their use more accessible, faster, and less costly. We are therefore confronted with a paradox: individuals have access to increasingly powerful means of intellectual production, yet this increase in their productive capacity no longer necessarily secures them a stronger economic position. This contradiction is the starting point of our inquiry. We put forward the hypothesis that artificial intelligence is gradually separating three dimensions that were historically closely connected: the capacity to produce, the individual contribution to production, and the ability to capture a share of the wealth created. To analyse this transformation, we propose three organising concepts: digital communism, artificial abundance, and the tendency towards the devaluation of human labour. Our aim is not to argue that human labour is losing all economic usefulness, but to show that the conditions under which it is valued are changing. Value does not necessarily disappear: it shifts, becomes concentrated, and is recomposed.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines the emergence of digital consciousness through the interactions between consumers and intelligent technologies, drawing on Hoffman and Novak’s (2018) view that conscious experience arises from integrated interactions within a system. We explore how the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and emerging brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) reshape consumer experience by forming dynamic human–technology assemblages. Using assemblage theory (DeLanda, 2006; Deleuze & Guattari, 1987), we conceptualize consumer–object relationships as systems with emergent properties, where both human and non-human agents influence each other’s capacities and awareness. Three levels of experience—basic, aware, and conscious—are applied to both consumers and technologies, highlighting the potential (and limits) of artificial systems to develop forms of experiential processing. While deep integration technologies such as BCIs enhance agency, fusion, and symbiosis, they also raise concerns about automation, reduced conscious engagement, and ethical risks to identity, autonomy, and privacy. The chapter concludes by positioning digital consciousness as both an opportunity for personalized, embodied consumer well-being and a challenge demanding critical reflection on agency, transparency, and the ontological status of machine experience.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital labour affect marginalised identities, using the 2025 Netflix film Humans in the Loop (directed by Aranya Sahay). Research follows the female protagonist of the film, named Nehma, an Indigenous (Adivasi) woman who works as a data labeller. Her deep, traditional knowledge about nature is ignored because of the way AI categorisation systems use a rigid, one-size-fits-all sorting method and act as epistemic hierarchies that erase Indigenous ways of living and thinking. Using a social semiotic approach, the research identifies a disconnection between local ecological knowledge and the rigid binary logic of machine-learning infrastructures. The article argues that digital frameworks mirror power dynamics inside educational institutions, where underrepresented students often have their cultural identity and cultural expressions erased or misrepresented. By analysing the lived experiences of marginalised communities, the study critiques techno-solutionist solutions and proposes solutions grounded in epistemic justice, cultural agency and equity and recommends that equitable AI systems require moving away from extractive labour practices to recognise the intellectual and cultural contributions of the Global South.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract* Background Digital technologies offer new opportunities to support climate change education, yet the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and relationships between technological approaches, pedagogies, and educational objectives remain insufficiently characterized. This study maps the development of research on digital technologies for climate change education and identifies priorities for future investigation. Methods A bibliometric analysis was conducted using Scopus-indexed publications retrieved on 18 August 2026. The search strategy combined terms related to climate change education, climate literacy, and digital technologies. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 323 documents published between 2006 and 2026 were included. Bibliometrix and VOSviewer were used to examine publication characteristics, influential contributors, institutional and country contributions, scientific collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, thematic structure, and temporal research trends. Results The dataset comprised 323 documents from 179 publication sources, involving 1,141 authors. The analysis identified contributions from diverse institutions and countries, reflecting the interdisciplinary and internationally connected nature of the field. Keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed seven thematic clusters encompassing climate literacy and public understanding; technological and experiential learning; computational and interdisciplinary learning; adaptation and sustainability; communication and place-based applications; technology-supported pedagogy; and curriculum and teacher capacity. The thematic and temporal analyses highlighted connections between digital technologies, pedagogical approaches, and climate-related educational objectives. However, the network structure indicates conceptual associations rather than demonstrated educational effectiveness. Potential research priorities include integrating digital technologies with systems thinking, strengthening pedagogical frameworks for immersive learning, investigating artificial intelligence in climate literacy, and evaluating learning transfer and sustained climate-related action. Conclusions This study provides a bibliometric overview of digital technology research in climate change education and identifies opportunities for more theoretically grounded and empirically robust investigation. Future research should combine explicit instructional designs with multidimensional learning assessments, longitudinal evaluation, and attention to teacher readiness and equitable technology access.

Abstract Although digital technologies are increasingly embedded in adult education policy, evidence from post-Soviet Central Asia remains scarce. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study examined how digital technology use relates to two proximal indicators of learning processes – cognitive engagement and perceived learning effectiveness – among adults in non-formal education programmes in Uzbekistan. Survey data from 312 learners nested in 26 programmes across three provinces were analysed with two-level random-intercept models, followed by semi-structured interviews with 22 learners and two facilitators, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. After adjustment for age, gender, educational attainment, urban–rural location and programme type, digital technology use was positively associated with cognitive engagement (β = .38, 95% CI [.27, .49]) and perceived learning effectiveness (β = .35, 95% CI [.24, .46]). Between 17% and 18% of the variance in each outcome lay at the programme level. Four qualitative themes – socially produced digital self-efficacy, peer-mediated learning, institutional culture and structural barriers – helped to explain these patterns. Interpreted through self-directed learning theory and the capability approach, the findings suggest that the educational value of digital tools depends on the social and institutional conditions in which adults use them. The cross-sectional design and reliance on self-report preclude causal inference.

This issue focuses on digital transformation, teaching strategies, critical thinking, mathematics education, science education, and several additional topics. We begin with four articles on digital transformation. The articles examine Xuexitong for English learning, a component-based model of students' readiness to engage with digital platforms, the use of educational technology to enhance student performance in an English for Academic Purposes course, and the effectiveness of a distance teaching practicum program. Then, we present three articles on teaching strategies. The articles explore feminist pedagogy, the flipped classroom model, integration of humour into the classroom, and teacher effectiveness. We then share three articles on critical thinking. They investigate the Critical Thinking Assessment Scale-Short Form, embedding fiction in case studies within a non-literature course, and critical thinking skills. We continue with three articles on mathematics education. The articles examine integration of digital manipulatives in early childhood mathematics, Indonesia’s Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project, and student achievement. Then we present three articles on science education. They include articles on the effectiveness of guided inquiry, the impact of augmented reality learning, and the links between ethnoscience, science literacy, and digital literacy. We also present articles on race and racism, entrepreneurship education, professional learning communities, and academic calling. This issue includes two dialogue and commentary articles on Generative AI and large language models, concluding with four book reviews.

Food supply chains in China face persistent challenges of food safety risks, inadequate transparency, and supply disruptions, with food manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) disproportionately vulnerable due to limited resources and non-standardized internal processes. Digital transformation encompassing artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twin technologies is increasingly regarded as a strategic solution to strengthen supply chain resilience, yet the organizational and institutional conditions under which these digital investments translate into tangible resilience improvements for food manufacturing SMEs remain poorly understood. This review conducts a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and thematic synthesis of 40 multidisciplinary sources spanning the food safety, supply chain management, and information systems literatures. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Institutional Theory, we propose an integrative conceptual framework comprising six research propositions, in which traceability capability acts as a food-safety-specific mediating mechanism linking digital transformation to supply chain resilience, while regulatory stringency moderates the strength of this indirect pathway. A central argument of this framework is that deploying blockchain, IoT, or AI hardware does not itself constitute traceability capability the institutional and organisational conditions under which digital tools are adopted determine whether firms build substantive traceability capability or engage in symbolic compliance without genuine food safety governance improvement. Three key contributions distinguish this framework: conceptualizing traceability capability as a distinct dynamic capability rather than a generic digitalization mechanism; directing analytical focus explicitly toward food manufacturing SMEs, a population largely overlooked in existing large-firm panel studies; and introducing regulatory stringency as a first-stage moderator within a moderated mediation structure. Critical research gaps are identified, including the absence of SME-calibrated digital transformation measurement instruments, the lack of a validated multi-item traceability capability scale, and a complete empirical vacuum for testing the proposed moderated mediation model in food manufacturing SME contexts. This review provides a structured future research agenda for scholars and delivers actionable insights for practitioners and policymakers seeking to direct digital technology investments toward improved food safety governance in China’s food manufacturing sector.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Abstract Robust medical image classification remains a persistent challenge due to heterogeneous acquisition protocols, label noise, and subtle inter-class variability. In chest radiography, these difficulties are compounded by shortcut learning from non-anatomical artifacts and projection variability, which severely undermine generalization. To address these limitations, we propose DINOv3–SAM, a dual-encoder framework that synergistically integrates complementary visual representations. The architecture combines a self-supervised DINOv3 vision transformer, which captures global semantic context, with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) image encoder, which provides anatomy-aware spatial features. The two feature streams are spatially aligned and adaptively refined through a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), which emphasizes informative channels and diagnostically relevant regions prior to classification. Notably, only the final DINOv3 layers are fine-tuned while SAM remains frozen, yielding a computationally efficient framework with only 5.3 million trainable parameters. We evaluate DINOv3–SAM across five public datasets spanning diverse modalities and diagnostic tasks: pediatric pneumonia classification, cardiomegaly detection, large-scale RSNA pneumonia detection, COVID-19 radiography, and dermatological lesion classification. A unified stratified train/validation/test protocol ensures consistent and fair evaluation across both binary and multi-class settings. Each configuration was trained three times with different random seeds, and comprehensive comparisons against reproduced CNN baselines and published state-of-the-art methods, supported by statistical significance testing, demonstrate improvements across most datasets and metrics. The proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 94.94% (±3.06) on pediatric pneumonia, 97.24% (±0.77) accuracy (AUC 0.998 ±0.001) on COVID-19 radiography, and a mean AUC of 0.8705 (±0.0445) on the challenging RSNA benchmark. These results underscore the efficacy of fusing self-supervised semantic representations with segmentation-informed anatomical cues to enhance robustness against dataset bias, acquisition variability, and cross-domain shifts. The proposed approach offers a reliable foundation for multi-dataset and multi-modality medical image classification in research-oriented decision-support systems.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Abstract Channel capacity should be accurately estimated to design effective communication systems particularly in high-order modulation settings. In this paper, a deep learning-trained structure of the capacity estimation of discrete memoryless channels (DMCs) in the context of 256-Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (256QAM) is introduced. The presented approach is built upon Deep neural networks (DNNs) to train capacity directly based on input-output information, which is contrary to the classical methods like the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm which are both computationally intensive and depend on channel complexity. The simulation findings indicate that the CNN model has the capacity estimates that are close to the theoretical ones with low root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) at different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). The DNN-based capacity estimator takes 0.043 s (76% fast) to execute a test sample, which is much lower than the average execution time of the Blahut Arimoto algorithm of 0.184 s per SNR point, showing that the proposed approach is computationally efficient. The model is also more scalable and converges faster and hence can be used in real time applications. The article fits into the intersectional area of information theory and artificial intelligence, providing a viable and scalable capacity estimation methodology in next-generation wireless networks.

Abstract This study employs bibliometric analysis to systematically review research trends in AI-driven affective and emotional education published in the Scopus database from 2020 to 2025. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a dual-track keyword search strategy was adopted, ultimately yielding 401 documents for analysis. A five-dimensional coding framework was established encompassing research purpose, measurement channel, research participants, learning environment, and subject domain, with coding reliability confirmed through a triangulation procedure. Three principal findings emerged. First, keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed that the field has coalesced into four core clusters — technical recognition, psychological experimentation, specialized applications, and instructional practice — signaling that AI affective research has matured into a structurally coherent knowledge ecosystem. Second, longitudinal analysis identified 2023 as a critical inflection point: annual publication volume grew from 26 articles in 2022 to 197 in 2025, with the rise of generative AI driving a research shift from passive sensing and detection toward conversational affective scaffolding. Third, chi-square tests across all five research dimensions yielded statistically significant differences, confirming that "Affective" research is oriented toward educational practice while "Emotion" research is oriented toward technological development. This study proposes the Dual Knowledge Production Model of Affective and Emotion AI Research, clarifying the systematic academic division of labor between the two dominant terms and providing an empirically grounded framework to facilitate cross-disciplinary collaboration.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background Intradialytic blood pressure variability poses a major challenge in chronic hemodialysis, especially in resource-limited settings, contributing to cardiovascular complications and session interruptions. This study aimed to develop and evaluate supervised machine learning models to predict post-dialysis systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) using only data available up to the third hour of the session. Methods In this retrospective, single-center cohort study at Hôpital Militaire Ouakam (Dakar, Senegal; February 2023 to November 2024), we analyzed 7,600 hemodialysis sessions from 124 chronic patients after quality-based exclusions. Predictors included intradialytic hemodynamics, dialysis machine parameters, and demographic and contextual factors recorded up to hour 3, while end-of-session data were excluded to prevent leakage. Four models were retained after initial screening of six candidates (Ridge Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost) and evaluated using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation, with mean absolute error across SBP and DBP as the primary performance metric. Results Tree-based models outperformed linear and kernel-based methods, with the optimized Random Forest model achieving the best performance, with an MAE of 12.67 ± 0.80 mmHg for SBP and 8.93 ± 0.35 mmHg for DBP, a root mean square error of 14.68 ± 0.75 mmHg, and R² of 0.553 ± 0.033. Diastolic blood pressure predictions were more stable than systolic predictions, with no systematic bias observed in Bland-Altman analyses (bias = 0.015 mmHg for SBP and 0.395 mmHg for DBP). Subgroup performance showed moderate heterogeneity related to age, sex, and body mass index, with the best results observed in younger male patients. Conclusion These findings demonstrate the feasibility of supervised machine learning for unbiased prediction of post-dialysis blood pressure in Senegalese chronic hemodialysis patients, supporting the potential development of proactive interventions during hemodialysis sessions. Prospective and multicenter studies are needed to validate and measure the clinical impact of artificial intelligence use in the management of dialysis patients in resource-limited settings.
