documents.abstract: This chapter examines how AI is transforming emergency response and crisis management by strengthening emergency preparedness, communications, real-time coordination, and organizational resilience. Building upon the ESH Management System and PRIM governance framework introduced in earlier chapters, it demonstrates how AI enables organizations to shift from reactive emergency response to predictive, intelligence-driven preparedness. This chapter explores the application of machine learning, predictive analytics, computer vision, NLP, digital twins, IoT technologies, robotics, and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems to improve hazard detection, threat assessment, emergency planning, resource allocation, and decision-making. AI-supported emergency communications are presented as a means of delivering real-time, location-specific alerts, multilingual notifications, and coordinated situational awareness that improve response effectiveness during rapidly evolving events. This chapter also examines the role of robotics in hazardous and inaccessible environments, demonstrating how autonomous systems can support search and rescue, damage assessment, environmental monitoring, and post-incident recovery while reducing responder exposure to dangerous conditions. Real-world case studies, including British Petroleum’s Geospatial AI Engine and AI-assisted satellite analysis during the 2025 Myanmar earthquake response, illustrate how AI can accelerate damage assessment, improve operational coordination, and enhance emergency planning across both industrial and natural disaster settings. Collectively, these capabilities demonstrate how AI strengthens organizational preparedness, improves emergency response effectiveness, supports continual organizational learning, and enhances resilience within modern Emergency Preparedness Programs and crisis management systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to monitor and assess capture fisheries, addressing persistent limitations of conventional observation systems that are labor‐intensive, costly, and difficult to scale. Despite rapid technological expansion, AI development in this field remains fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its structure and direction. This study aimed to map the development, intellectual structure, and thematic evolution of AI research in capture fisheries monitoring and assessment through a bibliometric and synthesis‐based review of Scopus‐indexed literature (2015–2026). Following a documented, large language model‐assisted screening protocol with human verification, a final corpus of 495 journal articles was analyzed using an integrated bibliometric and science‐mapping workflow. Results showed a marked, near‐exponential increase in publication output after 2020. Rather than confirming a pre‐defined three‐domain structure, keyword co‐occurrence analysis revealed that the field's thematic organization follows technical task type (detection, classification, and operational/vessel management) more closely than application domain, with acoustic AI failing to form an independent thematic cluster and representing the smallest share of the corpus (8.1%), behind visual AI (44.0%) and vessel monitoring (28.9%). For synthesis, we nonetheless compare the field across three functional categories visual AI for fish detection and measurement, vessel monitoring using AIS/VMS data, and acoustic survey support finding that the field is methodologically converging around a shared AI/ML toolkit while remaining largely siloed at the technical‐application level. Although research productivity remains heavily concentrated in China (85.9% of records) and international collaboration is limited (23.64%), the field is moving beyond isolated proof‐of‐concept studies toward more operational, management‐relevant applications. Overall, this study provides an evidence‐grounded, rather than assumed, understanding of how AI research in capture fisheries is thematically structured, and identifies acoustic AI and cross‐domain integration as priority areas for future development toward fisheries‐oriented, evidence‐based management.

Quality Control (QC) and Quality Assurance (QA) are key elements in the pharmaceutical sector. They help to ensure the safety, efficacy and consistency of medicines. This article discusses the purpose of QC and QA for pharmaceutical manufacturing in the modern era and outlines their development, principles and problems relating to the application of technology and universal quality standards. The article reaffirms the need for continuous and seamless improvement in the maintenance of quality system improvements that are responsible for global health standards and that can be applied to licensed drugs in a wide range of settings, ensuring the effectiveness of medicines delivered to patients in a sustainable manner. QC and QA are important components in pharmaceutical production. Their combined function is to ensure that all products are safe, efficient and reliable. As the industry evolves and moves toward digitalization, automation and data-centric systems, QC and QA evolve from reactive functions to predictive and preventive tools. Continuous improvements, regulatory compliance and the adoption of technology will shape the future of pharmaceutical quality. This paper also analyzes the beneficial use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the pharmaceutical sector throughout all phases, from drug discovery to drug development, as well as in various departments. Besides necessitating less human labor, it also improves the efficacy of clinical research and pharmaceutical output while diminishing the likelihood of mistake. The report examines the existing challenges in the implementation of AI within the pharmaceutical sector. Furthermore, it evaluates existing challenges and proposes remedies.

documents.abstract: Pharmacovigilance has evolved from a system based mainly on spontaneous adverse drug reaction reporting into a multidimensional discipline that combines global case-report databases, active surveillance, pharmacoepidemiology, digital health records, patient-generated information and advanced analytics. This expansion is necessary because pre-authorisation trials cannot fully identify rare, delayed, interaction-related or population-specific harms that emerge during routine use. This narrative review examines the architecture of international pharmacovigilance, major surveillance platforms, signal-detection approaches, clinical and regulatory risk assessment, and current developments in artificial intelligence and real-world evidence. The World Health Organization Programme for International Drug Monitoring and VigiBase provide a framework for cross-national learning, while regional and national systems such as EudraVigilance, the United States Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System and India's Pharmacovigilance Programme of India support local reporting and regulatory action. Disproportionality methods, including the reporting odds ratio, proportional reporting ratio, information component and empirical Bayes approaches, are useful screening tools but do not establish causality or incidence. Active surveillance and well-designed non-interventional studies can strengthen signal evaluation by supplying denominators, comparators and longitudinal outcomes. Artificial intelligence can assist case processing, coding, duplicate detection and pattern recognition; however, biased data, limited external validation, weak explainability and automation errors require human oversight. Recent ICH E2D (R1) and M14 guidance further emphasise fit-for-purpose safety data and harmonised study methods. The review concludes that effective pharmacovigilance depends not on data volume alone but on reliable reporting, transparent analysis, timely risk communication, equitable global participation and practical measures that improve patient outcomes.

Purpose This paper presents the empathy-based bilingual digital pedagogy (EBBDP) model, a practice-informed framework developed through the author’s experience in remote teaching of accounting and taxation during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. It aims to show how pedagogical empathy can be translated into bilingual and digitally supported teaching practices intended to strengthen engagement, accessibility and emotional safety in virtual learning environments, particularly within technical education. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a reflective-practice methodology grounded in lived teaching experience within Portuguese vocational and professional training. It draws on pedagogical documentation, autoethnographic reflection and iterative adaptation of instructional strategies. The model integrates empathy, bilingual inclusivity and digital co-creation as central pedagogical pillars, illustrated through concrete examples using tools such as Google Workspace, Canva, Padlet and ChatGPT to support collaborative learning and formative assessment. Findings The reflective analysis identifies structured emotional check-ins, bilingual scaffolding, digital co-creation and multimodal assessment as practices through which pedagogical empathy may support accessibility, belonging and sustained participation. These practice-based interpretations are presented as conceptual propositions for future empirical testing rather than as measured effects. Originality/value This paper contributes to post-pandemic digital pedagogy by positioning empathy as a core teaching competence rather than a soft skill. It offers a conceptually grounded yet practice-driven model that translates pedagogical empathy into a structured set of bilingual, relational and digitally supported teaching practices, thereby bridging theory and classroom experience in technical education.

Industrial infrastructure in Saudi Arabia is undergoing expansion and renewal with the environment being as much a factor as the infrastructure itself with exposure to extreme heat, flash flooding, complex supply chains and highly interdependent utility services. Traditional HSE (health, safety and environment) arrangements will only go some way towards reducing the number of discrete incidents and will not in any way guarantee the continued function of the essential infrastructure in the face of a compound disruption. This is a critical integrative review of how occupational health, process safety, environmental protection and asset resilience can be managed as one decision system across the industrial project lifecycle. A total of 30 peer reviewed papers published between 2020 and 2025 were purposefully selected for this study, including three which were specifically Saudi focused. These were subjected to a thematic analysis looking at hazard pathways, institutional controls, operational dependencies and recovery capabilities. The synthesis of the findings identifies five persistent disconnects: compliance at the project level versus continuity at the network level; metrics of occupational injury versus metrics of major accident precursors; environmental assessment versus operational safeguards; information gathering versus accountable decisions; and controls in the construction phase versus controls for long term adaptation. In response to these disconnects the paper proposes an integrated resilience governance model which links critical function mapping, dynamic HSE risk assessment, protective barriers, cross operator coordination and performance based learning. Indicators are specified to support the model but are not presented as validated field thresholds. The contribution of this work is a testable management architecture rather than a claim of any measured national performance. It provides a framework which could be used by owners, regulators and delivery partners to help prioritise the interventions that will jointly protect workers, communities, the environment and the continued function of the key services.

Introduction Population-based cancer screening programmes facilitate early cancer detection, thereby contributing to reduced cancer-related morbidity and mortality. However, participation rates have declined in recent years, with lower uptake particularly evident among invitees in vulnerable positions. This decline can be partly attributed to information that is insufficiently tailored to individual needs and literacy levels, and to the fragmented nature of the screening offer. To address these barriers, this study explored two strategies: (1) developing a personalised screening portal presenting information in an accessible and tailored manner, and (2) improving the alignment and potential integration of screening programmes. Methods Four co-creation sessions were conducted with 13 screening invitees and eight experts in cancer screening and human factors engineering. Two sessions focused on prototyping a screening portal and two explored the potential for combined screening. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed thematically using inductive coding. Results Invitees and experts emphasised the need for a digital portal offering concise, empathetic, personalised, and phase-specific information. Invitees perceived added value in combined screening, whereas experts considered organising all screenings at a single location and time to be infeasible in the current context. Both groups agreed that integrating information provision across programmes would be valuable and feasible. Discussion These findings suggest that integrating information across screening programmes is a meaningful and achievable step towards improving accessibility and supporting informed decision-making, particularly for invitees in vulnerable positions.

This concluding chapter presents a practical roadmap for implementing AI within an ESH Management System by integrating project management, governance, organizational change, and continual improvement into a unified implementation strategy. Building upon the PRIM framework developed throughout the book, this chapter demonstrates how organizations can systematically acquire, deploy, govern, and sustain AI technologies while minimizing operational, regulatory, and organizational risks. It examines the application of established project management principles, including scope, cost, schedule, and risk management, together with a structured example illustrating how PRIM can guide AI model acquisition and implementation. This chapter introduces the PRIM AI Maturity Model as a governance framework for assessing organizational readiness and advancing AI integration from initial experimentation to optimized, continuously improving capabilities. Recognizing that successful AI adoption depends as much on people as technology, this chapter explores change management, workforce training, communication strategies, and the Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability Reinforcement (ADKAR) model to foster employee trust, competency, and organizational acceptance. It also addresses AI records management, regulatory compliance, ethical considerations, transparency, and accountability as essential components of responsible AI governance. Finally, this chapter examines the influence of AI on organizational culture, emphasizing that sustainable transformation requires leadership commitment, ethical decision-making, and continual learning. Collectively, the concepts presented throughout this chapter reinforce the central theme of the book that AI achieves its greatest value when governed through the PRIM framework and embedded within a mature ESH Management System, where technology, governance, leadership, and organizational culture work together to improve worker safety, environmental stewardship, operational resilience, and long-term organizational excellence.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This chapter establishes the foundational principles of Environmental, Safety, and Health (ESH) Management and introduces the essential concepts that underpin the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern ESH practice. It distinguishes between individual ESH Programs and an integrated ESH Management System, demonstrating how management systems provide a structured, risk-based framework for governance, regulatory compliance, continual improvement, and organizational performance. This chapter examines the roles of leadership, organizational culture, worker commitment, and systematic issue management in creating effective ESH Programs while emphasizing internationally recognized management system standards, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 14001 and ISO 45001. It also introduces the principles of risk management, including hazard identification, risk assessment, prioritization, mitigation, monitoring, and continual reassessment, as fundamental components of an effective ESH strategy. Together, these concepts provide the organizational and technical foundation necessary for understanding how AI can responsibly enhance hazard recognition, decision-making, predictive analytics, compliance, and overall ESH performance throughout the remainder of the book.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Traditional industrial and organizational paradigms treat human capital as an elastic, indefinitely renewable asset. However, under chronic operational strain, biological systems undergo progressive, non-linear degradation governed by thermodynamic and epigenetic constraints. Within the Science 4.0 framework, this paper formulates the “Human Factor” as an exhaustible, dissipative natural resource operating far from thermodynamic equilibrium. We introduce a conceptual non-equilibrium thermodynamic model that relates chronic socio-technical load to increased biological dissipative demand and internal entropy production (σ_ent), challenging the organism’s buffering capacity. To explore this framework at the molecular interface, we deploy the Nuclear Receptor Subfamily 3 Group C Member 1 ( _NR3C1_ ) gene as an illustrative biological pilot. We model how sustained operational strain relates to cumulative allostatic load and context-dependent epigenetic remodeling at the _NR3C1_ promoter (exon 1F), which in some experimental and clinical contexts has been associated with attenuated glucocorticoid receptor expression, represented within the model as a reduction in the normalized Bioenergetic Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR*_bio). Using a Shannon-inspired informational capacity formulation, we analyze the conditions under which homeostatic feedback loops lose fidelity. Modeling the human factor through thermodynamic and kinetic resource-depletion curves provides a hypothesis-generating foundation for sustainable ergonomics, regenerative governance, and the preservation of biological integrity in high-demand socio-technical architectures.

Purpose Global health discourse has increasingly focused on achieving universal health coverage, yet the occupational health needs of the workforce delivering these services remain systematically neglected. This paper aims to address the systematic neglect of the occupational health needs of female health-care providers – principally nurses and midwives – in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The paper makes particular reference to Sub-Saharan Africa. It develops an integrative multilevel conceptual model that explains how this neglect is produced, transmitted and amplified and proposes implementable multilevel responses. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a structured integrative literature review, reported in line with the PRISMA 2020 statement, and conducted for the purpose of conceptual model development. Eighty-six sources retained from six databases and grey literature repositories were synthesised through a codebook-style thematic analysis. It draws on the Social Determinants of Health (SDH) framework, Moral Injury Theory, the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model and the Health Equity Framework. Findings The synthesis suggests that macro-level structural determinants are proposed to produce the foundational architecture of provider neglect. Meso-level organisational factors are proposed to transmit macro-structural neglect into the lived realities of individual providers. Micro-level clinical stressors appear to amplify the intermediate consequences experienced by individual providers beyond what structural and organisational factors alone imply. Gendered structures operate as a cross-cutting context conditioning every level of the model. Feedback loops link deteriorating health system outcomes back to macro- and meso-level conditions. Dismantling provider neglect is therefore proposed to require simultaneous interventions at all three levels of the model. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual paper, the proposed model is not empirically tested. It requires empirical validation through quantitative and qualitative studies across different health-care settings, particularly in LMICs. Cross-national comparative studies across Sub-Saharan African, South Asian and Latin American contexts would test the model’s generalisability. Longitudinal studies tracking the same provider cohorts over time would help examine the proposed sequence and feedback loops. Practical implications The paper emphasises the necessity for national governments, health ministries and institutions and policymakers to establish comprehensive occupational health programmes, dedicated health insurance schemes for providers, workplace wellness initiatives, mental health services and financial protection mechanisms. It specifies responsible actors, implementation priorities and measurable outcomes for each recommendation. International development partners, global health donors and multilateral organisations should integrate health-care workforce welfare into health systems-strengthening investments. Social implications The study reframes health-care providers as a vulnerable population whose health needs are often overlooked within health-care systems. It contributes to sustainable development goals 1 (end poverty in all its forms everywhere), 3 (ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all), 8 (productive employment and decent work and economic development for all), 10 (reduce inequality) and 16 (provide access to justice for all). Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study to integrate macro-, meso- and micro-level explanations of health-care provider neglect within a single conceptual model that embeds gender-specific mechanisms and feedback loops in its connecting structure. It reframes this neglect as an equity and social justice issue rather than a management problem. It extends Moral Injury Theory into the domain of occupational health exclusion. It repositions the SDH framework as a tool for analysing occupational health inequalities among the health workforce itself.

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by students and is reshaping the way information is accessed, processed, and utilised for academic work and everyday purposes. As the use of AI technologies continues to expand, there is a growing need to discuss the ethical implications associated with the use of generative AI among LIS students. This study employed a narrative review method to analyse and synthesise evidence from existing scholarly literature obtained through various library resources and online databases on the Internet. The study identified several ethical implications regarding the use of generative AI among LIS students, which include breaches of academic integrity, plagiarism risks, misinformation, output bias, privacy and security concerns, reduced critical engagement with learning materials, overdependence on AI systems, fabricated references, and so on. The findings revealed that ethical use of generative AI requires LIS students to critically evaluate AI-generated content, acknowledge AI assistance where necessary, and maintain responsibility for the accuracy and originality of their academic work. The study showed areas for future research directions in ethical concerns of generative AI use among LIS students for responsible AI use in academic practices.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Aim: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized by dental students and specialty candidates as supplementary tools for examination preparation. However, their reliability in specialized clinical domains requiring analytical reasoning remains underexplored. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the accuracy, reliability, and inter-model agreement of three contemporary reasoning-focused LLMs in answering Periodontology questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination (DUS).Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional in silico study, 100 multiple-choice Periodontology questions administered in past DUS sessions (2012–2026) were selected. The questions were presented in isolated sessions without prior contextual prompting to three models: OpenAI GPT-5.5 Thinking, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 (adaptive thinking), and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro. Responses were scored dichotomously against official answer keys. Overall accuracy rates were compared using Cochran's Q test, pairwise agreement was assessed via Cohen's Kappa (k) coefficient, and shared error distributions were analyzed using a two-tailed Binomial test (p 0.05), ChatGPT and Gemini selected the identical incorrect distractor in all 5 questions they mutually failed (100% shared error rate; p = 0.0625).Conclusion: Contemporary reasoning-capable LLMs demonstrate high accuracy and substantial inter-model consistency on specialty-level Periodontology questions. Nevertheless, the presence of concordant errors indicates shared algorithmic blind spots, underscoring that AI outputs must be supplemented by specialist oversight and evidence-based verification in dental education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in healthcare depend on both data quality and model design. However, the predictive integrity of datasets is rarely assessed. Publicly available resources for critically ill children remain scarce. The Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database remains, to the best of current knowledge, the only open-access resource focused on pediatric critical care research. Methods This study evaluates the predictive potential of the PIC database. After applying strict cohort selection and data preprocessing, mortality risk was analyzed using statistical analysis through univariate Odds Ratio (OR) to measure associations, and machine learning (ML) models interpreted through SHAP values to assess feature importance and model behavior. Results ML experiments showed moderate but limited predictive performance for mortality. CatBoost performed best, with an AUC of 0.8521 (0.8414–0.8627) on the hold-out test set, but low sensitivity (42%) limited its ability to identify non-survivors. These findings suggest dataset-related constraints that reduce clinical reliability. Most relevant variables were minimum lactate, maximum lactate, mean respiratory rate, maximum hematocrit, and minimum urea. Conclusion Analysis showed that PIC lacks essential physiological data, highlighting the limits of current pediatric databases and the need for richer multicenter datasets to enable more robust, clinically applicable AI models. Impact Provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the PIC database, assessing its suitability for machine learning-based predictive modeling. Identifies key clinical variables and data gaps that influence the reliability of AI–based mortality prediction and model performance. Underscores the need for richer, multicenter pediatric ICU databases for research that incorporate essential physiological and neurological indicators. Demonstrates the value of combining statistical association and AI interpretability methods to assess the predictive integrity of clinical datasets.

Students with learning disabilities need clear, direct, and useful writing feedback. However, teachers often find it hard to provide this consistently because of time and workload pressures. New developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) might help improve both the frequency and quality of feedback for students. Still, we know very little about whether AI-generated comments are valid or useful for struggling writers. This qualitative study looked at teachers' views on writing feedback from the AI-SCORE automated writing evaluation tool. Nine upper elementary and middle school teachers took part in two focus groups. They reviewed AI-generated feedback on student informational writing. They also discussed its clarity, teaching value, and suitability for students with disabilities. Thematic analysis revealed several areas for improving AI-generated feedback. Teachers want more guidance on specific revisions, language that suits students’ development, a consistent tone, and alignment with writing goals. They shared cautious optimism, noting that AI feedback could enhance teaching capacity and provide more practice opportunities for students, if it meets their needs. The findings stress the importance of teacher involvement, the potential benefits of AI for writing instruction, and key factors for creating AI tools that effectively support students with learning disabilities.

INTRODUCTION: Scaling and root planing (SRP) is traditionally the initial therapy in the treatment of periodontitis. So, clinicians should develop a solid theoretical knowledge of instrumentation and the required clinical skills. This study aimed to evaluate the educational exposure, pedagogical perceptions, and the level of clinical and technical knowledge of undergraduate dental students regarding SRP to identify knowledge gaps. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted between January and August 2025 with 105 students distributed into G1 (1st-3rd semester), G2 (4th-7th semester) and G3 (8th-10th semester). Data were collected using a digital form containing epidemiological and technical questions in dichotomous and multiple-choice formats, addressing identification of periodontal instruments, specific clinical indications for SRP instruments, operative principles, post-SRP clinical effects, grasp techniques and professional-patient ergonomics. Statistical analyses were performed using Chi-square and G tests (p ≤ 0.05). RESULTS: Significant differences in theoretical and practical exposure to SRP were observed (p < 0.0001). Technical performance demonstrated significant knowledge gaps; for instance, only 63.8% correctly identified Gracey curettes, and approximately half demonstrated mastery over sickle scalers (52.4%) and less than half for hoes (46.7%). There were significant differences among groups in distinguishing between surgical and non-surgical instruments (p < 0.0001). A deficit in operative skills was noted, particularly in professional-patient ergonomics, with 53.3% correct answers, and in grasp technique, with a correct response rate of 6.7%, indicating gaps in preclinical psychomotor training. CONCLUSION: The study reveals potential gaps in the retention of technical-scientific knowledge among students, suggesting that exploring continuous reinforcement strategies may benefit the teaching of scaling and root planing in northern Brazilian dental schools.

Extensive delegation of productive and intellectual activities to artificial intelligence may reconfigure the conditions under which people encounter tasks, develop purposes, and interpret their participation. This paper investigates existential self-perception through the distinction between external outcomes and the relational histories of their production and experience. It differentiates ontological existence, prereflective ownership, experienced agency, narrative continuity, interpersonal recognition, and institutional standing. Its central proposition concerns the distribution of experiential participation: AI mediation can alter access to intermediate decisions, resistance, feedback, and revision, even when the resulting output remains comparable. The analysis extends this proposition to the development of purposes, ecological and aesthetic encounters, absorbed attention, and the temporal organization of habits and recollection. It proposes conditional tests of the relational-feedback account while considering output quality, novelty, task demands, and material conditions as competing influences. Meaningful participation can occur with reduced explicit self-monitoring, while the significance of an episode may develop through subsequent relationships and reflection. A complementary research program proposes episode-level elicitation, bounded comparisons of delegation, longitudinal observations, and studies of shared environments. These designs distinguish experiential reports, observable activity histories, and institutional conditions, enabling investigation of how different arrangements of delegation shape opportunities for participation. The post-labor counterfactual provides a setting for examining diverse experiences and forms of self-understanding amid changes in productive necessity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Accurate identification of primary suspect drugs in adverse event reports is a critical component of post-marketing pharmacovigilance and serves as a foundation for downstream signal detection activities. However, causal attribution in spontaneous reporting systems such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is inherently challenging. Traditional expert-based assessments are resource-intensive and difficult to scale, highlighting the need for complementary, reproducible approaches. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of large language models (LLMs) in identifying primary suspect drugs in adverse event reports against an expert reference standard. Methods Fifty FAERS case reports were randomly selected for evaluation. Three clinical pharmacy experts established the reference standard by adjudicating the primary suspect drug(s) for each case. LLM-based evaluations were conducted using multiple prompting strategies and model configurations. The performance of LLMs, pharmacy student evaluators, and original FAERS primary suspect designations (ROLE_COD) was assessed by calculating hit rates against the expert reference standard. Results The original FAERS designations demonstrated limited accuracy against the expert reference standard, with a hit rate of 0.778. In contrast, LLM-based assessments achieved consistently high hit rates ranging from 0.867 to 0.920 across diverse prompting strategies and model configurations. Student evaluators achieved a comparable hit rate of 0.872; however, LLM-based evaluations exhibited greater internal consistency and markedly shorter response times. Conclusion LLM-based evaluations demonstrated high accuracy against expert assessments and favorable efficiency relative to student evaluators. These findings highlight the potential utility of LLMs as scalable, readily accessible decision-support tools in pharmacovigilance workflows.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Electricity theft imposes substantial revenue losses on utility operators and threatens smart-grid stability. Existing detection methods struggle with scarce labelled anomalies, distribution shift, and opaque decision boundaries that hinder forensic auditing. This paper proposes SSTCL-AD-XAI, a self-supervised temporal contrastive learning framework with explainable artificial intelligence for anomaly detection in hourly electricity consumption data. A two-layer LSTM encoder is first pre-trained via InfoNCE contrastive loss with stochastic augmentations — random hour masking, multiplicative scaling, and additive Gaussian noise — and then fine-tuned with Focal Loss under a leakage-safe protocol in which validation data serve only for model and threshold selection. Evaluated on a combined synthetic and SGCC corpus of 42,872 samples over 10 independent seeds, the framework attains a mean F1-score of 0.914, a mean ROC-AUC of 0.975, and a mean PR-AUC of 0.949. It significantly outperforms six unsupervised detectors — LOF, One-Class SVM, HBOS, Deep Autoencoder, DAGMM-like Autoencoder, and Transformer Autoencoder — at Wilcoxon p=0.002, and exceeds a supervised BiLSTM reference in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC while matching its F1-score. Source-wise evaluation confirms that performance is carried by the real SGCC data (SGCC-only F1 0.914), and a 5% prevalence stress test quantifies the deployment operating point (Recall 0.955, Precision 0.357). Multi-seed ablation identifies self-supervised pre-training as the dominant performance driver. Sequence-aware attribution via Integrated Gradients and temporal occlusion, computed exclusively on SGCC samples, confirms midnight consumption (H1) as the most discriminative forensic feature, and quantitative embedding metrics (silhouette 0.548; Davies-Bouldin 0.786) verify moderate and consistent class structure. The framework demonstrates promising potential for transparent electricity theft detection and provides a foundation for future validation in operational smart-grid environments.

Abstract Generative AI tools are increasingly present in language learning, yet their role in second language (L2) reading remains underexplored. This study investigates how intermediate German learners engaged with ChatGPT during interpretive reading using a three‐condition design with a Grimm fairytale. The study examines the relationship between AI access and reading performance, patterns of use or resistance, and students' ethical and motivational interpretations of AI‐mediated reading. Generative AI emerged as a negotiated presence that learners approached with curiosity, caution, or resistance. Required AI use was associated with reduced differences in comprehension outcomes across proficiency levels, whereas optional use revealed diverse strategic, reluctant, and value‐driven stances rooted in ethical concerns, discipline‐specific norms, and a desire to maintain interpretive autonomy. Students who routinely used AI in other courses engaged more selectively in German, suggesting AI practices may be shaped by disciplinary contexts. The findings support guided, reflective AI integration while valuing learner resistance.

Abstract Rapid urbanization has intensified health and social inequities through the uneven distribution of infrastructure, services, and public space. In St. Louis, Missouri (USA), these disparities remain geographically concentrated and rooted in long-standing patterns of racial segregation and disinvestment. This study examines how spatial inequities shape urban livability by integrating scalable artificial intelligence (AI) methods with community-based insights. We applied a vision–language model, supported by a large language model, to classify micro-scale built-environment features from 7,848 Google Street View segments, and conducted semi-structured interviews with residents and stakeholders. The AI analysis revealed baseline infrastructure such as street lighting (85%) and continuous pavements (77%), but very low coverage of universal-design features: curb ramps (9.7%), pedestrian crossings (7.1%), and walk signals (4.3%). These deficits were significantly associated with lower median incomes and higher proportions of non-Hispanic Black residents. Qualitative findings confirmed and contextualized these patterns, linking them to historical redlining, fragmented governance, and everyday experiences of constrained mobility and safety. By combining scalable AI tools with community narratives, this study demonstrates that spatial inequities are both visible in the physical streetscape and embodied in daily life. Methodologically, it advances the use of VLM and LLM-enabled pipelines for urban audits; conceptually, it reframes livability metrics through the lens of spatial equity; and practically, it provides a replicable framework for equity-centered planning.

Face presentation attacks threaten the dependability of facial biometric authentication, particularly when conventional RGB cameras are exposed to print and replay artefacts. Existing texture descriptors are computationally attractive but remain sensitive to noise, illumination variation, and image degradation, whereas many deep architectures require substantial data and processing resources. Prior studies establish the value of handcrafted texture features, Binary Statistical Image Features (BSIF), auxiliary-supervised networks, and foundation-model approaches, but the reviewed evidence does not explicitly assess Gaussian linear filtering as a face-image preprocessing stage before BSIF extraction. This study adopted is structured into sequential and interconnected phases were integrates Gaussian linear filter with sigma 1.0, eight-bit BSIF coding, a normalised 256-bin histogram, feature standardisation, and support vector classifier (SVC). Experiments use OULU-NPU, with five-fold validation on SiW and CASIA-FASD. On the reported OULU experiment, the system achieved 87.28% accuracy, 65.83% precision, 76.70% recall, a 70.85% F1-score, and 93.39% ROC-AUC, compared with 73.50% accuracy and 0.724 ROC-AUC for raw-pixel SVC. Mean accuracy was 83.69% on SiW and 95.05% on CASIA-FASD. Gaussian filter- BSIF features provide a compact and discriminative representation for software-only face presentation attack detection. The work demonstrates a lightweight preprocessing-texture-classification pipeline and reports both predictive and computational measures. Future studies should enhance the robustness, scalability, adaptability, and efficiency of face presentation attack detection by integrating advanced preprocessing techniques, multimodal biometrics, lightweight artificial intelligence models, and adaptive learning strategies.

Due to the integration of mechanical, electronical and software functions in modern products, virtual product development is becoming increasingly important. In this context, virtual prototyping in particular can benefit from the visualization of CAD models of a system in virtual reality (VR) simulations, as this can support activities such as ergonomic assessments and design reviews in the early stages of development. Furthermore, managing the growing complexity of products can be supported by creating consistent system models following the Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach. By combining system models, created by SysML modeling syntax, CAD models, and VR simulations, benefits for the virtual model-based product development can be generated and information as well as model consistency can be improved. This article introduces a tool for the integration, simultaneously visualization, and automated linking of SysML and CAD models in an interactive VR environment. The tool can support design review and validation processes by displaying CAD objects and the associated information of the system model in one virtual environment at the same time. The focus of the exemplary tool application in this article is the validation of system requirements defined in a SysML model through the examination of a true-to-scale CAD model in VR. As a build-in feature, the validation results can be documented in the VR simulation and returned back to the SysML modeling tool so that they can be taken into account in further system development. The tool validation demonstrates potential for virtual reviews, early requirement validation, and bidirectional data exchange.

ABSTRACT The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.
topics: Mathematical and Theoretical Epidemiology and Ecology Models
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Fear of negative evaluation (FNE) is typically conceptualized as a concern about interpersonal judgment, but as artificial intelligence (AI) systems become more interactive, users may also anticipate evaluation from AI itself. This study examined whether FNE from humans (FNEH) and from AI (FNEA) are differentially associated with technology-acceptance perceptions. University students and faculty (N = 203) completed parallel measures of FNEH and FNEA, along with measures of perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and perceived enjoyment (PE) for intelligent chat services. Structural equation modeling showed that FNEH was negatively associated with PU and PE, whereas FNEA was negatively associated with PEOU and PE. The two PE associations did not remain significant after Holm adjustment. Direct comparisons showed that FNEH and FNEA differed significantly only for PEOU, with FNEA showing the stronger negative association. Their associations with PU and PE did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that the source of anticipated evaluation may be particularly relevant to perceived ease of interacting with AI. The study extends research on FNE to human–AI interaction and highlights the importance of examining evaluative concerns in users’ perceptions of AI-based technologies.

ABSTRACT Aims To evaluate the feasibility of a flipped learning low back training programme among nurses, focussing on ergonomic knowledge, exercise performance and confidence, and participant satisfaction. Background Work‐related low back pain is a common occupational health problem among nurses. Comprehensive training programs including promotion of ergonomic knowledge, proper exercise performance, and confidence may enhance safe musculoskeletal practice. Design Feasibility study. Methods Twenty registered nurses were recruited from a graduate nursing programme between 2022 and 2023 with prior clinical experience. The training programme used a flipped‐learning approach, incorporating evidence‐based low back exercises and gamified strategies. Meanwhile, ergonomic knowledge was assessed post‐programme and at 1‐year follow‐up, the exercise performance was rated during training and confidence in back exercise performance was self‐reported at follow‐up. Participant satisfaction was also measured. Results Participants demonstrated high ergonomic knowledge (mean score 71/100) after training, which remained satisfactory at 1‐year follow‐up (64.4/100). Peer scores of 13 low back exercises ranged from fair to excellent. Self‐confidence in performing the exercises 1 year later ranged from 7 to 9 out of 10, reflecting sustained ability to properly perform the exercises. Participants' satisfaction was high, indicating acceptance and perceived value in the programme. Conclusions The flipped learning–based low back training programme was feasible for nurses and supported retention of ergonomic knowledge, correct exercise performance, and sustained confidence 1 year after training. High participant satisfaction further supports its acceptability, suggesting its potential for future implementation in clinical musculoskeletal practice. These observations are exploratory given the descriptive study design; hence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This scoping review maps how artificial intelligence is conceptualized and used in educational leadership and management and examines the transition from technology adoption toward human-AI leadership. Following established scoping-review guidance and PRISMA-ScR, records from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed published or officially available online from 2022 to the final search date in 2026 were screened; items assigned a 2027 bibliographic year were eligible only if already available online before the cutoff. Of 747 records identified, 183 duplicates were removed and 323 records underwent title-and-abstract screening. Full texts were sought for 81 reports; two could not be retrieved, 79 were assessed for eligibility, and 50 studies were included. Four themes emerged: leadership readiness and capability; AI-augmented leadership practice; organizational conditions and institutional transformation; and human-AI agency, governance, and ethical boundaries. The evidence favors augmentation rather than autonomous substitution, with human judgment remaining central to accountability. The review proposes a five-stage Human-AI Educational Leadership Continuum integrating individual capability, organizational readiness, governance, and decision authority. The review was limited to three databases and English-language articles, and the evidence base remains methodologically heterogeneous and largely cross-sectional or context-specific.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This working paper sets out a research framework for examining value that may go unused in the Qurbani (sacrificial animal) system, and a proposed "Smart Waqf Fund" model for governance, innovation and social development. It links Sharia grounding, operational governance, legal characterisation, economic feasibility and social development, and keeps established facts, research hypotheses and institutional proposals clearly separate. Part One sets out the framework: the institutional idea of preserving the asset and benefiting from its fruit; a six-stage method for measuring utilisation in the Qurbani chain; a proposed research farm; temporary cash waqf and waqf units; digital administration; the GoSmart knowledge alliance; human wellbeing; education through the Awqaf animal family; and a research roadmap. Part Two contains supporting research files on risk management, a preliminary comparison of seven jurisdictions (New Zealand, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, Kuwait, Bahrain and Malaysia), multilingual awareness and artificial intelligence, AAOIFI Governance Standards 14 and 15, the fiqh question of temporary cash waqf and qard hasan (pending before the 12th Forum on Waqf Fiqh Issues), economic feasibility, research and vocational training, and publication rights. Status: a developmental research working paper, open to critique. It is not peer reviewed and is not a fatwa, a legal opinion, an offer document or an invitation to participate financially. It reports no measured results. No waqf units are offered in any jurisdiction. All figures are editorial illustrations, not charts based on measured data. Two editions are deposited: the Arabic original and a full English translation, each as an A4 PDF. Licence note: published under CC BY-NC 4.0. The Awqaf New Zealand name and logo are excluded from the licence; third-party material, including AI-assisted illustrations, remains subject to its own terms.

Abstract: Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates how communication anxiety and psychological need satisfaction relate to the use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, for communication tasks (e.g., writing emails, drafting messages, and preparing scripts). Using a three-wave panel survey of participants from the United States and South Korea, we examined both between- and within-person dynamics. Results showed that individuals with higher trait-level communication anxiety tended to use ChatGPT more frequently for communication tasks, whereas within-person fluctuations in anxiety did not predict greater use. ChatGPT use was positively associated with the satisfaction of basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence, and relatedness – and this need satisfaction, in turn, was associated with greater psychological reliance on ChatGPT. Importantly, need satisfaction further mediated the relationship between ChatGPT use and psychological reliance at both within- and between-person levels. Cultural comparisons revealed that US participants exhibited stronger momentary effects, while Korean participants showed more stable, trait-based patterns. These findings highlight the role of LLM-based chatbots as need-supportive communication tools that may become integrated into users’ communication practices over time, with implications for theories of AI-mediated communication, cross-cultural research, and the design of human-AI communication systems.

The higher education sector has seen the emergence of several technological advancements over the past two decades. These include learning management systems, massive open online courses, and the latest on the market: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). This paper aims to make a critical review of the shift from Digital Transformation to AI-driven education as a whole. The paper particularly emphasizes the shift of the digital transformation from being an administrative phenomenon to being more of a central feature in education. The paper summarises the literature on the concepts of digital transformation, the implementation of generative AI, and adaptive learning and AI ethics in the teaching and learning process, based on peer-reviewed papers that were mainly published in Scopus and Web of Science from 2019 to 2026. There are three themes that are repeated in the literature. First, AI in education is a further step towards digital transformation in which capacity building processes are substituted with independent decision making. Second, personalisation, accessibility and efficiency are opportunities, not equally accessible or equally taken up, nor equally realised; and these opportunities go first to the best resourced institutions.

Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly visible in everyday financial activities. Students and consumers now encounter automated financial recommendations, digital investment platforms, personalised financial information and AI-based tools when making or evaluating financial choices. This changing environment raises an important question for Commerce education: is conventional financial literacy sufficient when financial information is increasingly mediated by algorithms? The present study examines financial literacy, AI literacy and awareness of ethical issues associated with AI-supported financial applications among Commerce students, and investigates their relationship with algorithmic financial decision quality. The study follows a descriptive and analytical research design and considers 250 student observations. Data were examined using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression. Four major constructs were considered in the analysis: financial literacy, AI literacy, ethical awareness and algorithmic financial decision quality. The findings show that financial literacy recorded the highest mean score (M = 3.56), while AI literacy recorded a comparatively lower mean score (M = 3.33). AI literacy demonstrated the strongest correlation with algorithmic financial decision quality (r = .705, p ≤ .01), followed by financial literacy (r = .623, p ≤ .01) and ethical awareness (r = .605, p ≤ .01). The regression model explained 67.2% of the variation in algorithmic financial decision quality. AI literacy emerged as the strongest predictor (β = .443), followed by financial literacy (β = .376) and ethical awareness (β = .199), with all three predictors statistically significant at p ≤ .001. The findings suggest that financial knowledge remains essential, but it needs to be complemented by the ability to understand, question and evaluate AI-generated financial information. Commerce education therefore needs to move towards an integrated approach in which financial literacy, AI competence and ethical awareness support independent and responsible financial judgement.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in urban governance, infrastructure and design, yet urban theory still lacks a clear language for analysing the scale asymmetries through which these systems operate. This article develops Gulliver Urbanism as a conceptual framework for understanding how AI reshapes urban power when it processes information, acts, and coordinates across cognitive, temporal and spatial horizons that exceed ordinary human capacities and institutional rhythms. Moving beyond Frankenstein Urbanism’s emphasis on rebellion and loss of control, we argue that the central problem of contemporary AI urbanism is scale asymmetry within co-constituted human and machine assemblages. The framework comprises six dimensions: cognitive scale, temporal scale, spatial scale, governance asymmetry, autonomy and agency and human response. It synthesises scholarship on AI urbanism, urban political economy, infrastructural urbanism, posthumanism, law and scale, supported by AI governance frameworks and vignettes on Hangzhou City Brain, robotaxis and generative design. The article conceptualises the urban as a constitutive condition of AI scale asymmetry, where algorithmic systems encounter infrastructure, land, mobility, public services, municipal authority, social difference and collective life. Across these domains, the key challenge is how to govern systems whose capacities outpace human oversight while remaining embedded in corporate, legal and political arrangements. We argue that effective responses require mixed-intelligence governance and temporal dignity: arrangements that subject algorithmic operations to democratic oversight, contestation and human-paced deliberation. Gulliver Urbanism explains how AI reconstitutes urban life by reorganising infrastructures, municipal authority, spatial relations, design imaginaries, public services and everyday citizenship.

documents.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) is changing how design alternatives are generated in fashion film design learning, enabling students to obtain large numbers of comparable and iteratively refinable visual outcomes within a short period. However, expanded generative capacity does not, by itself, determine how learners interpret, evaluate, experiment with, and select among uncertain outcomes. In this human–AI collaborative creative environment, empirical evidence remains limited on whether learners’ design-related psychological tendencies form a distinguishable multidimensional structure that is comparable across learning stages. Design Thinking Mindset (DTM) provides a multidimensional psychological framework for addressing this issue. Methods Drawing on Vignoli et al.’s DTM framework, this study examined five dimensions—Uncertainty and Risk, Empathy, Experimentation, Abductive Reasoning, and Creative Confidence—through a cross-sectional survey of 409 first-year and third-year students from three Chinese universities who had experience with AIGC fashion film design projects. Confirmatory factor analysis and measurement invariance testing across year groups were used to examine the five-dimensional structure and its measurement comparability, followed by latent mean comparisons. Results The five DTM dimensions formed a correlated yet distinguishable structure and demonstrated measurement comparability across year groups. Third-year students had significantly higher latent means on all five dimensions, with the largest descriptive standardized difference point estimates observed for Abductive Reasoning and Creative Confidence. Discussion These findings provide empirical support for the applicability of five selected DTM dimensions in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning and reveal distinct patterns of self-reported psychological tendencies across year groups. From an educational perspective, the results suggest that AIGC-supported design education should attend not only to the generation of creative alternatives but also to learners’ psychological orientations toward uncertainty, experimentation, audience understanding, creative reasoning, and confidence in creative work.

Abstract This study compares traditional translation and post-editing with generative-AI-assisted translation in Arabic–English translation education. Drawing on 68 task records completed by 58 undergraduate students through EduApp, it examines observable effort, textual intervention, and implications for translation competence. The findings indicate that AI-assisted tasks involved significantly more written or entered characters and a higher length ratio, but no statistically significant difference in task completion time. Qualitative analysis suggests a shift from local correction to broader reformulation, including more formal institutional phrasing and syntactic restructuring. The study concludes that AI-assisted translation redistributes rather than eliminates student effort and requires evaluative and interactive skills alongside established translation abilities.

Machine learning models predict badminton strokes, but the practical value of tactical recommendations depends on whether players can execute them. Player capacity can change within matches and across successive tournament matches. Based on structured searches of eight bibliographic sources, this narrative review synthesizes tactical modelling and badminton physiology to examine the evidence needed for executable recommendations and coaching use. We distinguish five types of claim (description, prediction, prescription, adoption and outcome), each requiring a different form of validation. Most tactical studies focus on prediction or the development of coach-facing interfaces. Amongst tactical studies with assessable inputs, 30% included match-context variables, such as score, but no explicit measure of player state. Very few used explicit physiological variables, and none reported fitting or validating models using measured player state during match play. Beyond developer-led evaluations, our search identified no study in which practitioners received model-derived recommendations and an outcome was recorded. Physiological studies document metabolic demand, neuromuscular fatigue, perceptual changes under load and cumulative effects across successive matches. Several report maintained performance, so whether fatigue alters feasible or optimal tactics remains a testable hypothesis. We distinguish candidate inputs for use during play, principally video-derived estimates of player-specific movement load, from variables suited to research and post-match monitoring. We also propose a reporting checklist separating information studies can report now from requirements that need new data. This framework specifies the evidence needed to evaluate whether recommendations are executable, whether coaches adopt them and whether measurable outcomes follow.

In many educational contexts, classroom disciplinary practices are often dominated by punitive approaches, in which mistakes are responded to criticism or punishment in the name of maintaining order and discipline. Such practices may discourage participation, reduce students’ confidence, and limit meaningful engagement, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning where students are already vulnerable to anxiety and fear of making mistakes. However, alternative approaches that emphasize support rather than punishment remain underexplored, especially in relation to their broader impact on classroom dynamics. Grounded in Behaviourist theory by Skinner, this study investigates whether and how Positive Reinforcement enhances student engagement in EFL classrooms. A sequential explanatory mixed-method design was employed involving 105 junior high school students in Indonesia. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-surveys, followed by qualitative interviews with five students to further explain the statistical findings. The quantitative results showed a statistically significant improvement in students’ engagement (p < .001) after the implementation of Positive Reinforcement, with a large effect size (r = 0.86), indicating a strong practical impact. The qualitative findings further revealed improvements in five major areas: (1) behavioural engagement, (2) cognitive engagement, (3) emotional safety and confidence, (4) peer interaction and communication, and (5) student-teacher relationships. These findings suggest that shifting from punitive to supportive practices not only enhances individual student engagement but also contributes to the development of more positive and supportive classroom dynamics in EFL learning environments.

Purpose This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can improve organizational crisis management as firms increasingly operate in a polycrisis marked by overlapping pandemics, geopolitical conflict and rapid technological change. It maps AI capabilities to the before, during and after phases of the crisis lifecycle. Design/methodology/approach This narrative/conceptual review synthesizes empirical and theoretical scholarship on AI in crisis management across management, information systems and crisis communication journals. It integrates evidence on early warning, anticipation, social media analytics, crisis communication and resilience into a lifecycle framework. Findings Before a crisis, AI-driven early warning systems can predict disruptions weeks in advance and help mitigate losses. During a crisis, natural language processing supports situational awareness, and generative AI accelerates communication. After a crisis, social listening and simulation support learning, while deepfake defense protects reputation. Benefits are conditional on governance maturity and complement, rather than replace, human judgment. Practical implications Firms should adopt AI proactively but judiciously for sensing, triage and rehearsal, guided by governance readiness rather than novelty. They should also invest in data governance and interoperability. Organizations should keep accountability and ethical judgment visibly human where trust and empathy matter most. SMEs benefit from modular, centrally supported adoption pathways. Originality/value This paper integrates AI and crisis management into a lifecycle framework centered on the governance conditions that enable AI to improve outcomes. It advances two propositions: (1) AI’s value shifts from augmenting anticipation to substituting risk as authorship becomes visible, and (2) governance maturity moderates, rather than predicts, AI’s crisis-management payoff.
